item.title: Harrison Smith Returns — And the Cap Gets Complicated
item.description: Harrison Smith's $12.25M return, cap concerns, bold predictions, and an NFL Rivalry Weekend pitch.
item.content:encoded:
Harrison Smith is back — and Tyler Forness is not doing the fanboy version. On a Labor Day Real Forno Show, Forness and producer Dave Stefano unpack the Hitman’s one-year Vikings return, the cap squeeze it creates, and a CFL-inspired pitch for a real NFL Rivalry Weekend before Week 1 vs. Green Bay.

The contract is the headline. Smith’s deal is structured as roughly $8 million base value with $4 million in per-game roster bonuses and $4 million in playoff incentives that max near $16 million only if Minnesota wins the Super Bowl. Play all 17 and he lands around $12.25 million. Forness supports the player getting paid — “Harrison Smith got his money, and on a human level, good for him” — then flips to the team view. Minnesota had about $8.8 million in cap space before the signing. After bonus, per-game money, and the leftover dead cap from the spring release, operating room looks closer to $2 million. “That’s not enough to operate a season,” Forness said. “You have to have more than that.”

The football case is layered. Forness will not pretend Smith is replaceable by a draft pick. “Harrison Smith’s brain cannot be found on the street. It cannot be drafted.” Bringing him back lets Josh Metellus stay in his own role instead of becoming a full Harrison clone. The worry is the other half of the job. Flores’ packaging still needs legs after the snap — the A-gap look that bails to single-high. “If he can’t do that anymore, then you can just absolutely destroy it. Jared Goff, Matthew Stafford, they’ll kill it.” Stefano pushed the conductor argument: “The Vikings are not paying for Smith’s legs, they’re paying for his pre-snap chaos.” Forness’s answer: chaos is worthless if quarterbacks can just throw at the 37-year-old. He also walked the ugly cap chess — Blake Cashman, T.J. Hockenson, Will Fries, Andrew Van Ginkel — where pushing money out only works if you actually want those players long term.

They also spent the open on a CFL Labor Day Classic idea: lock one mid-October weekend as Rivalry Weekend, same divisional pairings every year, trophies, merch, promotion that actually sells the fight. “Everything is pro wrestling. It is what you make it.” Then they read fan bold predictions: Kyler Murray leading the team in rushing, Justin Jefferson chasing 2,000 yards and the Triple Crown, Dallas Turner leading the league in strip sacks, Will Reichard drilling 70 in Mexico City, Super Bowl 61 matching the franchise’s 1961 founding year.

Key points:

  • Smith return: one year, ~$12.25M if he plays 17, max via Super Bowl incentives
  • Cap: thin operating space after Jefferson, Darrisaw, and Murphy already restructured
  • On-field: brain and communication vs. possible athletic drop
  • Metellus stays Metellus if Smith is the communicator
  • Rivalry Weekend pitch: fixed October week, not Thanksgiving
  • Fan spice: Murray rushing title, Jefferson records, Turner strip sacks
  • Next on the network: Packers preview, Who Will Be King, Two Old Bloggers

Or on your favorite podcast aggregator.

Watch:

Watch the full Labor Day episode on Vikings 1st & SKOL / Bleav. Forness is not here to tell you the Hitman is automatically a win. He’s here to ask what $12.25 million costs in August flexibility — and whether Week 4 still looks like Week 1.

What do you think?

Is Smith the glue that holds Flores together, or the cap bill that shows up in November?

item.title: 5 Jets storylines to watch as 2026 NFL season begins
item.description: Here are five Jets storylines to watch during the 2026 NFL regular season...
item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing 3-14 campaign in 2025, the Jets get their 2026 season underway on Sunday afternoon, as they travel to face their former head coach Robert Saleh and his Tennessee Titans.

Plenty of changes have been made during the offseason, with many of the main building blocks still in place. These changes are not guaranteed to be effective, though and, if they backfire, it won't be long until we hear the familiar refrain of "Same Old Jets" from fans and media.

Here are five storylines to watch during the regular season...

Geno Smith's redemption story

For Geno Smith to return to the Jets organization after a decade away is improbable enough; especially given the ignominious nature of his departure. However, what would it be like if he could actually succeed in his second act?

"That would be like a story in a movie, right?" Smith has said, "Kind of like one of those superhero movies."

It's already remarkable enough that Smith ascended to a Pro Bowl level in Seattle after the Jets had all but written him off at the end of a disappointing and controversial four season run with the team. However, it's obvious that the 35-year old has matured and gained fresh perspective in his time away.

As he makes his return to New York, fresh doubts surround Smith, who once famously said "They wrote me off... I ain't write back though". He led the NFL in interceptions as he led the Raiders to the league's worst record in 2025.

In principle, the Jets have the offensive line stability, offensive playmakers and experienced offensive coaches that should make it feasible for Smith to bounce back. There are probably a few more twists and turns to come in this particular "movie," though.

Aaron Glenn feels the heat

Publicly, the Jets organization has thrown their support behind head coach Aaron Glenn, and preached patience and pragmatism as he needs the time to rebuild the Jets' roster and culture, not to mention their structures and processes.

However, ownership has earned a reputation for being impatient over the past few decades, so Glenn can't afford a slow start in 2026. The Jets initially looked competitive in Glenn's first season, losing two of their first three games on last second field goals to playoff contenders. However, they ended up losing their first seven games. Anything similar in 2026 is sure to get the vultures circling.

Glenn, who is taking over responsibility for defensive playcalling this season, added veteran coach Frank Reich to oversee the offense, and will take charge of a roster that looks considerably deeper than last year's following an active offseason.

While Glenn has repeatedly discussed the need for a long-term plan, the fact so many changes needed to be made does little to inspire confidence in how much progress has been made. He's going to need to produce tangible results sooner rather than later. 

The foundation is in place for the Jets to be more competitive this year, but Glenn still has a challenge ahead of him as he tries to get the Jets out of the losing habit. A couple of early wins would go a long way towards getting things moving in the right direction.

Can the new additions help the Jets change the losing habit?

Not only have the Jets been enduring a league-worst 16-year postseason drought, but they made history in 2025, which ended up being a season to forget. The Jets became the first team in NFL history to lose five games in a row by 23 or more points at the end of the season, and were also the first NFL team ever to go a full season without intercepting a pass. 

Nevertheless, the Jets have reloaded their roster this season with a mixture of veteran leaders and high-potential youngsters. Could this group help the Jets win games and restore relevance?

Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick give the Jets a pair of Pro Bowl talents who should help eradicate the kind of defensive breakdowns that defined last season. There's also hope for the future with rookie David Bailey bringing star potential to the pass rush. The offense wasn't neglected, though, with Smith bringing experience and two pass catchers selected in the first round to give him a better collection of weapons.

If these moves can transform the Jets into a competitive unit, we could end up seeing them flexed into a national game after all.

Will New York have a dominant special teams unit again?

Special teams coordinator Chris Banjo's unit was a rare bright spot in 2025, ranking among the best in the NFL.

New punter Austin McNamara was a revelation, backed up by an well-coached coverage unit that included some individual standouts. In addition, the return game was a difference-maker, with both Kene Nwangwu and Isaiah Williams making a series of big plays.

Most of the key contributors are returning for 2026, which bodes well, but there's one key omission. Kicker Nick Folk had a terrific 2025 season, but he signed for Atlanta and the Jets have cycled through several placekickers during the offseason to try to find an adequate replacement.

For now, Blake Grupe is on the roster and the recently-released Jason Sanders remains on the practice squad, but the Jets find themselves in the familiar position of entering a season with uncertainty at that spot.

Banjo and the Jets will be crossing their fingers that this doesn't come back to bite them.

Which returning Jets are primed for a breakout?

As part of their rebuilding process last year, the Jets traded away defensive stars Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner at the deadline, and have since parted ways with the likes of Quincy Williams, Jermaine Johnson and Alijah Vera-Tucker.

However, parts of the old nucleus remain. Garrett Wilson is back after an injury-plagued fourth season, and Breece Hall, perhaps surprisingly, signed an extension after posting the first 1,000-yard rushing season of his career. Could they ascend to new heights in Reich's offense?

Most experts are high on the young tackle pairing — Olu Fashanu and Armand Membou — to continue to improve, but a real boost would come from someone unexpected like wide receiver Adonai Mitchell or cornerback Azareye'h Thomas establishing themselves as a star.

Many of these players have seen plenty of losing during their time with the Jets. The challenge for Glenn and the other coaches will be to make the team competitive to create the conditions for these returning players to thrive and realize their full potential.

item.title: Myles Garrett expected to go for Rams on Thursday
item.description: Myles Garrett should be good to start the season, Van Jefferson finds a new home and more!

How excited must the NFL be to have this first ever NFL game in Australia happening, but they also get to have Garrett and Aaron Donald as major talking points for the event.

item.title: Who will lead the Titans in receiving in Week 1?
item.description: Which playmaker will lead the Tennessee Titans in receiving yards against the New York Jets in Week 1?
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans will make their 2026 NFL season debut by hosting the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium in Week 1 this Sunday. There’s so much to learn about these new-look Titans. Head coach Robert Saleh and the team’s new coordinators Brian Daboll and Gus Bradley will officially make their debuts.

The most important aspect of the Titans’ 2026 campaign is the development of sophomore quarterback Cam Ward. Coach Daboll is being tasked with overseeing his ascension. The Titans’ new-look passing game will finally be unveiled versus the Jets.

This is a deep receiving core in Tennessee. Carnell Tate was drafted at fourth overall to grow alongside Ward. Wan’Dale Robinson was signed in free agency for his ability to be a high-volume, reliable weapon. Calvin Ridley is also back, and Elic Ayomanor had an excellent training camp. The Titans are four-deep at receiver.

Who do you think will lead the Titans in receiving in Week 1? It’s an interesting question. Fans would love to see Tate explode after he failed to record a single preseason catch. Robinson should be Ward’s most reliable weapon, possibly leading the Titans in targets. Ridley is a big-play threat who once played in Daboll’s offense at Alabama.

Running backs and tight ends should also be heavily involved in the Titans’ passing attack. Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears, Gunnar Helm, and Daniel Bellinger will play notable roles in Daboll’s offense. Ward will be tasked with spreading the ball around to a plethora of players.

The Titans should also establish the run via Pollard and Spears. This Titans-Jets rematch is littered with revenge storylines. From Saleh to John Franklin-Myers, Jacob Martin, Jermaine Johnson, Solomon Thomas, and Tony Adams, Tennessee is loaded with former Jets players. Who leads the Titans’ new-look passing attack in receiving is another question.

item.title: Why Mike Tomlin is welcoming 'a little bit of performance anxiety' in new job
item.description: Mike Tomlin stepped down from the Steelers to become an analyst for NBC. He's dealing with 'a little bit of performance anxiety' in his new role.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL season will kick off on Wednesday, Sept. 9, when the Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots in a Super Bowl 60 rematch.

For the first time since 2006, Mike Tomlin will not be preparing for a season opener of his own with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Instead, the long-time NFL coach will be a part of NBC's coverage of the Seahawks-Patriots matchup, serving as an analyst for the network's "Football Night In America" pregame show.

The irony of Tomlin's new position is not lost on the 54-year-old, as he explained in a recent interview with Craig Melvin of "Today."

"I've trained myself over the years to tune out some of what I refer to as noise," Tomlin said. "Now, the noise is my business."

Tomlin spent 19 seasons as the Steelers' head coach, leading the team to a Super Bowl 48 win over the Arizona Cardinals while never logging a losing season. His 193 regular-season wins are tied with Chuck Noll, another Steelers legend, for the ninth-most in NFL history.

As such, Tomlin's move to the analyst's desk is marked change for him after he spent the last 25 years coaching in the NFL.

Even so, he wasn't exactly sure how to describe any type of learning curve he was facing during his transition to the broadcast world.

"I don't know, 'cause I have nothing to compare it to," the former Steelers coach said. "It's been a fun process to be a novice at something."

Tomlin already made his broadcast debut during the annual Pro Football Hall of Fame preseason game between the Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers.

Nonetheless, the 54-year-old explained that he is dealing with "a little bit of performance anxiety" as he acclimates to his role during the 2026 NFL season.

"It's good. I like that," Tomlin said. "I like being on edge. I like being the newbie."

Tomlin has also enjoyed getting some time away from the grind that came with the rigorous schedule required of an NFL coach.

"I never knew what I was missing," Tomlin said. "So it's a new world for me."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Why Mike Tomlin is welcoming 'a little bit of performance anxiety' in new job

item.title: The quiet shift reshaping the Cowboys
item.description: It’s becoming hard to ignore how Brian Schottenheimer is changing the culture of the Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys may have quietly changed what they’re looking for in a football player. Not necessarily bigger. Not necessarily faster. Not necessarily more talented.

Just more serious.

Call them “Serious Dudes“, with a hat tip to Voch Lombardi for the moniker.

It’s not a scientific category, and it’s certainly not a requirement that every player walk around the facility looking like he’s preparing for a tax audit. It’s more about how a player approaches the job: preparation, accountability, doing his assignment, competing through the whistle, and not needing every moment to become a personal statement.

The Cowboys have always had players like that. Every successful team does. What’s interesting is how many of them now seem to be showing up on this roster.

And that makes me wonder whether Brian Schottenheimer has quietly started putting more emphasis on a quality that doesn’t show up particularly well on a draft board or salary-cap spreadsheet: professionalism.

The new generation of Cowboys

Start with Tyler Booker: The second-year guard was identified as a natural leader before he had even played his first NFL season, then followed that up with more than 1,000 snaps and 14 starts as a rookie.

Now, just one year into his career, Booker is already part of the Cowboys’ 11-man Leadership Council. That’s not necessarily because he’s the loudest player in the room. It’s because the organization appears to trust him to help set the standard.

Then there’s Caleb Downs. Downs is an even more interesting case because the expectations attached to him go well beyond simply playing good football.

Dallas traded up to select Downs 11th overall, and the conversation around him quickly became about influence as much as ability. Mel Kiper called him a “culture changer,” while NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein described him as a “culture piece” for a Dallas defense that badly needed one.

But perhaps the most telling assessment came from inside the Cowboys’ locker room.

When DeMarvion Overshown was asked about Downs, he didn’t talk about giving a rookie time to adjust to the NFL. He said the Cowboys weren’t even looking at Downs as a rookie. They were looking at him as someone who could “change this defense around” and “change the culture.”

That’s a remarkable expectation to place on a player who hasn’t yet played an NFL snap.

And it tells us something about what the Cowboys think they drafted. Downs isn’t simply expected to be a good safety. He’s expected to be an influence. Of course, Downs hasn’t yet established himself as a locker-room leader. But the Cowboys expected that potential to be part of his value when they traded up to get him.

And then there is the rest of the next generation.

Jaishawn Barham might be the clearest example of the type. The rookie linebacker was one of the more talked-about players in training camp, and the description coming from the Cowboys themselves was almost tailor-made for this post: “all business.” Schottenheimer also highlighted Barham’s physicality, his ability to get off blocks, and his versatility.

Malachi Lawrence is a quieter example. The first-round pick hasn’t attracted anything like the attention surrounding Downs, but his early approach has been refreshingly straightforward: learn from the veterans, understand what it means to be a professional, and work on the technical details of his game.

That doesn’t prove Lawrence will become a leader in Dallas. It doesn’t even tell us what kind of personality he’ll have five years from now. But it is another example of the type of player the Cowboys appear to be bringing into the building.

Donovan Ezeiruaku is a slightly different case. There is plenty of evidence of the work ethic and football intelligence Dallas likes, and the second-year edge rusher has talked about the importance of standards and learning from veterans. The Cowboys’ training-camp coverage has also highlighted his knowledge and experience.

But Ezeiruaku also plays with an edge. His involvement in several training-camp fights was a reminder that taking football seriously doesn’t necessarily mean being emotionless. A Serious Dude doesn’t have to be boring.

He can be intense. He can be emotional. He can be loud. The distinction is what happens when the helmet comes off.

The veterans who changed the locker room

The pattern becomes more visible when you look at the veterans Dallas added.

Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark are probably the two strongest examples. Neither needed the Cowboys to teach them how to be professionals. They came with established reputations, extensive NFL experience, and Pro Bowl credentials.

Yet both quickly became central figures in the locker room. Williams arrived in the middle of last season, when the Cowboys’ defense was already in trouble. Nine months later, he has been elected one of only four team captains by his teammates. Clark was also voted a captain. The other two are Dak Prescott and Brandon Aubrey.

That’s worth noting because the Cowboys have made a distinction this year between their Leadership Council and their team captains. The four captains were chosen entirely by player vote, with Prescott, Williams, Clark, and Aubrey receiving the most votes.

Williams has also been unusually open about what he sees changing. After spending the final seven games of 2025 in a defense that was struggling badly, Williams recently described the defense’s progress as “night and day.” He credited the coaching, the talent, the daily competition, and the overall change in the way the unit approaches its work.

That’s exactly the sort of thing that makes the Serious Dude theory interesting.

It’s not just about individual personalities. It’s about what happens when you put enough of the right people together.

Kenny Clark fits the same mold. Williams has talked about Clark as someone who holds people accountable and does things the right way, both on and off the field.

Jalen Thompson provides another piece of the puzzle. The veteran safety was brought in to stabilize a secondary that badly needed it and was subsequently included in the Leadership Council.

Rashan Gary adds another veteran presence to the defensive front, while Cobie Durant brings experience, versatility, and toughness to the secondary.

Jonathan Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia are less obvious examples of the personality argument, but they matter in another way: they are experienced defensive linemen who add depth around Williams and Clark.

And that’s an important distinction.

Not every new player has to be a Serious Dude in the same sense. Some are simply evidence of a roster being built around more experience, physicality, versatility, and professionalism.

The pattern emerges from the combination.

Meet the Leadership Council

Perhaps the most tangible evidence that this is about more than individual impressions is the Cowboys’ Leadership Council.

The 11-player group consists of:

Dak Prescott
CeeDee Lamb
Tyler Smith
Tyler Booker
Jake Ferguson
Javonte Williams
Quinnen Williams
Kenny Clark
Rashan Gary
Jalen Thompson
Bryan Anger

That’s an interesting collection of players. It’s also interesting because Schottenheimer has made clear that this isn’t just a ceremonial group. He has said that the council could have included as many as 15 players, but he deliberately kept it smaller. More importantly, he described it as “their council, it’s not mine.”

The players are expected to bring issues from the locker room to the coaching staff and help solve problems before they become bigger problems. That’s a very different concept from simply naming a few captains for the coin toss. And it tells us something about what the Cowboys value in their leaders.

You don’t need to be the biggest star on the team. You don’t even need to have been there the longest. You need to be someone your teammates trust.

That helps explain why Booker is on the council after just one NFL season. It explains why Williams and Clark were elevated so quickly. It explains why Javonte Williams, who has spoken about the responsibility of bringing teammates along and being a voice for the locker room, is part of the group.

And it gives us another reason to be interested in Downs. He isn’t on the Leadership Council. He shouldn’t be. He’s a rookie. But the expectations surrounding him suggest that Dallas isn’t merely hoping he becomes a great player. The organization believes he has the potential to become one of the people who sets the standard.

That’s a pretty good definition of a Serious Dude.

Serious doesn’t mean boring

There is an important caveat here. The Cowboys aren’t suddenly trying to build a roster of robots.

CeeDee Lamb is still CeeDee Lamb. Dak Prescott isn’t exactly known for being a wallflower. George Pickens brings plenty of personality. And there is nothing inherently wrong with any of that.

Personality isn’t the problem. The question is what sits underneath it. The best version of this roster would not eliminate individuality, far from it. But it would make individuality secondary to the football.

When Schottenheimer talked about his satisfaction with the offseason, he didn’t limit his praise to talent. He specifically talked about the people the organization had brought in — not just what kind of players or coaches they were, but “the way they are as human beings.”

That is an interesting thing for a head coach to emphasize when discussing roster construction.

Talent gets you on the field. Character, professionalism, and accountability determine what happens once everybody gets there.

We’ve seen this before

The great Cowboys teams of the 1990s were not exactly short on personality. Michael Irvin was one of the biggest personalities in the NFL. Deion Sanders will always be Deion Sanders. Charles Haley brought his own particular brand of intensity.

But those teams also had Troy Aikman, Emmitt Smith, and Darren Woodson, and the Great Wall of Dallas. Different personalities. Different leadership styles. What they had in common was that the football came first.

That’s the useful lesson from those teams. Successful locker rooms don’t need to be boring, and they don’t need everyone to behave the same way. But they do need enough people who understand that the team is bigger than the individual.

The current Cowboys don’t have to recreate the 1990s. And comparing a handful of training-camp observations to one of the greatest teams in franchise history would be premature. But the resemblance in roster construction is worth noticing.

So, are the Cowboys becoming a team of Serious Dudes?

Maybe.

It’s far too early to say that Brian Schottenheimer and the front office have engineered some permanent cultural transformation. We’ve seen the roster change. We haven’t yet seen what happens when the games become meaningful. But the ingredients are there.

The Cowboys have added veterans such as Williams, Clark, Gary, Thompson, and Durant. They have drafted players such as Downs, Booker, Barham, Lawrence, and Ezeiruaku. They have created a Leadership Council that includes players from every part of the roster. And four of the players who received the most votes from their teammates are Prescott, Williams, Clark, and Aubrey.

None of that guarantees anything. But it does suggest that Dallas has become more deliberate about the kind of people it wants in the building. Maybe that’s the real shift.

The Cowboys aren’t getting rid of personality. They’re adding people who can keep personality from becoming the defining characteristic of the team.

And perhaps that’s what a Serious Dude really is. Not someone who never smiles. Not someone who never talks. Just someone who keeps his eye on the prize, sets the standard, and puts in the work to get there.

item.title: Pre-Snap Reads: What is the likelihood the Seahawks repeat as champions?
item.description: We pretty much did it once before, right guys? (cough, cough) How hard can it be?
item.content:encoded:
Our Seattle Seahawks ended up being a low-key/high-key dominant champion last season on their way to a convincing victory in the Super Bowl and their second Lombardi Trophy. This season, they return essentially the entire squad, save for a few depth pieces, and their starting running back, of course. What that means for our squad, we won’t know for several weeks. But, Wednesday will be a good indicator as to what and how this team will operate in 2026. New offense, same D (but, with some adjustments for injuries and scheme), and a special teams unit that once again can be truly special. How will it all end up coming together? item.title: Getting Defensive: Week 1 fantasy plays led by Jaguars, Chargers; top streaming defenses
item.description: Gary Davenport breaks down the fantasy football defense landscape headed into Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Are you ready for some football?

Of course you are.

We have successfully navigated the cold, dark months of the offseason, where there’s nothing to do besides watch the grass grow and occasionally talk to our families. Now, the sun is finally shining again—because on Wednesday the Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots in the first regular-season game of the 2026 campaign.

And that means that another season of fantasy football is here.

Hallelujah.

Just as with the other positions in fantasy, Week 1 lineup decisions where team defenses are concerned should be pretty straightforward. If you drafted an elite defense that has a shaky matchup in Week 1, you should have known that going in—just bite the bullet and roll them out. If you’re streaming matchup plays, then in theory you already know which favorable matchup you will be availing yourself of this week.

Don’t worry—we’ll all be confused and flailing wildly soon enough.

Gonna be another fun season.

GET YOUR FREE ROTOWORLD FANTASY FOOTBALL DRAFT KIT HERE!

Rotoworld Fantasy Football Draft Central 2026: Rankings, strategy, sleepers, and more
Your one-stop-shop for all of Rotoworld’s preseason content leading into fantasy football drafts.
  • Rotoworld Staff,

THE NO-DOUBTERS

Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Cleveland Browns)

Every September, we learn that some defensive matchups we thought would be awesome wind up being awful—and vice-versa. A lot can change on an NFL offense from season-to-season. But it can be said with the utmost of confidence that the Cleveland Browns will be terrible offensively in 2026, because NFL teams without quarterbacks tend to be. The Jaguars also tend to force teams to the air—Jacksonville has the best run defense in the league last season. In 2025, only the Las Vegas Raiders allowed more fantasy points per game to defenses than the Browns.

Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Arizona Cardinals)

The Chargers really don’t get enough credit for how well the team played defensively in 2025—the Bolts were a top-10 defense across the board and top-five in terms of yards allowed. Now, the Chargers open the season against an Arizona Cardinals team that was a goldmine for opposing defenses a year ago. The Redbirds allowed 59 sacks last year (second-most in the NFC), and the team gave up the seventh-most fantasy points per game to the position.

Pittsburgh Steelers (vs. Atlanta Falcons)

The Steelers have long been a consistently productive fantasy defense, and while the team had its ups and downs in 2025 Pittsburgh still finished a respectable eighth in fantasy points. Now, the Steelers will have a healthy T.J. Watt on the edge, and while Pittsburgh has legitimate questions in the secondary a Falcons team that will be starting Tua Tagovailoa at quarterback appears ill-equipped to exploit them. Look for Pittsburgh’s pass-rush to tee off. And for Tagovailoa to have a rough day in the Steel City.

Los Angeles Rams (vs. San Francisco 49ers)

Things could admittedly get weird for the Rams in the season-opener—this is a game being played in Australia on a Friday morning that will air in the United States on Thursday night because time travel. But this is a classic example of “if you drafted them, start them.” The Rams were sixth among defenses in fantasy points last year before adding Pro Bowl cornerback Trent McDuffie. And adding reigning Defensive Player of the Year and single-season sack king Myles Garrett. And adding some defensive tackle named Aaron Donald.

Philadelphia Eagles (vs. Washington Commanders)

The Eagles were once again stout defensively last year—Philly finished the season as a top-five scoring defense and was fifth in fantasy points at the position. There are potential issues along the defensive front with Jonathan Greenard banged-up to begin the season, but the team still has no shortage of talent at all three levels, and while the Commanders are hopeful 2026 will look more like 2024 than 2025, the Eagles defense is going to party at home like it’s 1999.

Denver Broncos (at Kansas City Chiefs)

On average this summer, the Denver Broncos were the third defense drafted, and with good reason—the team was second in the NFL in total defense in 2025, finished as a top-10 fantasy unit and led the league in sacks with 68. Starting out the season in primetime at Arrowhead against the rival Chiefs isn’t an ideal matchup to kick things off, but Kansas City has question marks on offense, including the health of quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Give Denver a go—and hope they help you finish Week 1 with a bang.

STREAMERS OF THE WORLD, UNITE!

Tennessee Titans (vs. New York Jets)

No one is going to confuse the Titans with the ’85 Bears anytime soon—Tennessee fielded a bottom-five scoring defense in 2026 and ranked outside the top-20 in yards allowed, and that defense isn’t exponentially better on paper this year than last. But neither is a New York Jets offense that is now led by Geno “Oh No!” Smith at quarterback. At the helm of the Raiders offense last year, Smith was sacked more times (55) than any signal-caller in the league and led all quarterbacks with 17 interceptions. Other than that, he was fine.

New York Jets (at Tennessee Titans)

The flip side of a bad game. Good times. Like the Titans, the Jets struggled defensively in 2025—Gang Green ranked 25th in the league in yards allowed and surrendered more points per game than any team in the AFC. However, the Titans had a tendency to make opposing defenses look good last season—the Titans were 31st in yards per game, 30th in points per game and surrendered the fourth-most fantasy points per game to defenses. The first team to score 13 here wins. Should make for great television.

Las Vegas Raiders (at Miami Dolphins)

The Raiders were not a good defensive team in 2025—Vegas surrendered the eighth-most points per game on the way to the NFL’s worst record. The Raiders invested a lot in that defense in the offseason though, bolstering the front and replacing both starting linebackers. This has less to do with the Vegas defense than it does their opponent in Week 1—the Dolphins have the most talent-deficient offense in the league, and that offense has spent most of the summer struggling mightily.

Green Bay Packers (at Minnesota Vikings)

The Packers fell apart down the stretch last season, and defensive lapses after edge-rusher Micah Parsons tore his ACL played a big part. The team will be without Parsons for at least the first month of this season as well, and after trading Rashan Gary the pass rush is a major question mark. With that said, the Vikings allowed more fantasy points per game to defenses last year than any team in the NFC, and while there’s a new quarterback in the Twin Cities that quarterback is not Fran Tarkenton.

Chicago Bears (at Carolina Panthers)

The Bears made the playoffs last year more in spite of the defense than because of it—Da Bears were the fourth-worst defense in terms of yards allowed and the 10th-worst defense in terms of points allowed. But the Bears were also highly opportunistic, piling up a league-high 33 takeaways on the way to a ninth-place finish in fantasy points. The Panthers were a playoff team last year, but with an 8-9 record—among 2025 playoff teams, only the Chargers were a better fantasy matchup for opposing defenses.

CAVEAT EMPTOR, FOLKS

Houston Texans (vs. Buffalo Bills)

The Texans have one of the best defenses in the NFL—full stop. Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter are arguably the best duo of edge-rushers in the game. A secondary that finished last year sixth in the league against the pass is loaded with talent. Houston was the first defense off the board in many fantasy drafts this summer. But know when you trot them out there in Week 1 that their fantasy output will be below-average (and then some)—the Bills gave up the sixth-fewest fantasy points per game to defenses a year ago.

Gary Davenport is a two-time Fantasy Sports Writers Association Football Writer of the Year. Follow Gary on X at @IDPGodfather.

item.title: 2026 NFL season preview, betting, odds: 1 bet I like for every NFC team
item.description: Matt Russell gives a wager he likes for all 16 NFC teams heading into the upcoming season.
item.content:encoded:
In Part 1 of our 32 bets for 32 teams ahead of the NFL season, we went up and down the AFC, looking for value in both the team futures and the player prop market; contemplating the statistical ceiling for some, and breaking down why others might not meet expectations. 

For Part 2, our attention turns to the NFC. Here is my favorite bet for all 16 teams:

Arizona Cardinals

Last season, we could feel positive statistical regression coming for Trey McBride touchdowns, as he was lined at 4.5 after a 2024 season where he scored just twice on 111 receptions. 

McBride scored 11 times. 

The market's done a better job adjusting to McBride than NFL defenses have, lining him at 6.5 touchdowns this season, but the Cardinals do have more red zone options this season. As a model of consistency with between five and 12 receptions in all but one game in 2025, and wanting to have a piece of McBride in some way, we'll bet on him to hit 100 receptions for a third straight season. 

Bet: Trey McBride over 97.5 receptions (-115, DraftKings)

Atlanta Falcons 

The Falcons took a big swing drafting Michael Penix Jr. in 2024, but it took less than two seasons for the concern over that move to come to fruition. Not only was he not a ready-made product as an older rookie, but his third torn ACL was the unfortunate answer to the questions about his durability. As a result, the Falcons signed Tua Tagovailoa on the cheap, hoping that one of them will have a career renaissance this season, but Kevin Stefanski brought Tommy Rees with him as offensive coordinator, and he has no track record for reclamation projects.

Defensively, the plan was that two first-round pass-rushers picked in 2025 would cause havoc for opponents who then had to throw into a secondary with A.J. Terrell and Jessie Bates. Jalon Walker tore his ACL in training camp, and James Pearce Jr. was suspended for the first half of the season. 

The Falcons are lined at 7.5 because there are game-breakers in place on both sides of the ball, but the players needed to put them in the best place to break games aren't there. 

Bet: Falcons under 7.5 wins (-140, DraftKings)

Carolina Panthers 

It's weird to say that the starting quarterback and the 2025 Offensive Rookie of the Year need to find a better connection, but Tetairoa McMillan caught only 57.3% of the passes thrown to him last season and went without a touchdown in nine of his first 10 games. Plus, that catch percentage actually went down in the final seven games of the season, a span where McMillan had five of his seven TDs. 

If Bryce Young and McMillan find a better connection in their second season together, that should translate to at least the same number of touchdowns for someone who profiles as the prototypical red zone target. 

Bet: Tetairoa McMillan over 6.5 TDs (-105, DraftKings)

Chicago Bears 

We'll mini-spoil one of THE WINDOW's cornerstone preseason betting articles, with a long-shot play on who might lead the NFL in receiving touchdowns — a category notorious for having surprise contenders. 

McBride made a run at catching the most touchdowns from the tight end position, tying for second in the league with 11. Colston Loveland could do the same this season. 

As a rookie, Loveland racked up the targets (48) in the Bears' final four games last season, and actually tied Rome Odunze and DJ Moore for the team receiving TD lead. With Moore gone, and both Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson talking a big game about Chicago's offense this season, this is a worthy look at a massive long shot. 

Bet: Colston Loveland most receiving touchdowns in the NFL (60-1, DraftKings)

Dallas Cowboys

If this happens, it will probably be insufferable — but, should a defensive overhaul work, featuring new defensive coordinator Christian Parker coming over from the Eagles, there's more than a non-zero chance that the Cowboys have a really good season. 

We already know that Dak Prescott's numbers will be there, so there's no need to sell anyone on whether he'd be the lead Cowboys' candidate for MVP, that is, if Dallas does win 12-plus games, the NFC East, and earns at least a top-two seed in the NFC. 

Classic Cowboys media attention will drive Prescott's candidacy past the top six choices on the oddsboard, all of whom come from the AFC. 

Bet: Dak Prescott to win MVP (12-1)

Detroit Lions

We had an under for a star quarterback in our AFC article, based on the double-premise of: A team being in more positive game-states than last season, while also expressing concern about injuries depressing their counting stats this season. 

In the NFC, the "pro" case for a Lions bounce-back season is how soft Detroit's schedule is, and if being the lookahead-line favorite in 14 of their first 15 games (and often by more than a touchdown) translates to fourth-quarter leads, Jared Goff will be in less shootouts this season. 

On the negative side, the Lions' offensive line is a far cry from when it was one of the best units in the NFL, buying time for Goff to find receivers down the field during his four straight seasons of 4,400-plus passing yards, and keeping him upright well enough not to miss a game.

Bet: Jared Goff under 4,099.5 passing yards (-110, Bet365)

Green Bay Packers

The Packers didn't fire Matt LaFleur, which, for a few days, seemed very much in play after another unceremonious postseason exit. 

Green Bay might be thrilled with an opportunity to blow a lead in the playoffs this season. 

Micah Parsons will miss at least the first four games as part of his return from an ACL tear, which compromises a defense that's invested in him being the centerpiece. 

Offensively, a great first season from Jordan Love set expectations that haven't been met since. A once-deep skill-position group has thinned out with wide receiver departures, Josh Jacobs' off-field issues and Tucker Kraft dealing with his own ACL rehab. 

In a tough division, and LaFleur potentially on his last chance, getting plus-money on the Packers to miss the playoffs is the way to fade Green Bay. 

Bet: Packers to miss the playoffs (+122, DraftKings)

Minnesota Vikings

In 2024, Sam Darnold was getting so much support in the media for Comeback Player of the Year, voters had to be reminded that the award is not supposed to go to players who come back from merely being bad. 

Kyler Murray was ostensibly hurt last season, which creates just enough plausible deniability for if he ends up being an equally good fit as Darnold was in Kevin O'Connell's offense (4,319 yards, 35 TDs).

Plus, Murray has never thrown for 4,000 yards or 30-plus touchdowns, so if he can replicate Darnold's season on a Vikings team that had nine wins with awful quarterback play last season, Murray will be the Comeback Player of the Year. 

Bet: Kyler Murray to win Comeback Player of the Year (+600, DraftKings)

Los Angeles Rams

It's not often a No. 2 running back is widely available in the season-long prop markets, but the line between Kyren Williams and Blake Corum is starting to blur. In 2024, when Corum was a rookie, he merely spelled Williams, getting out-carried 316 to 58 (and it was only that close because Williams missed a game).

Last season, though, the split tightened, to 259-145 (64.1% to 35.9%) — and even more in the final 11 games (164-116, or 58.5% to 41.5%). 

For the season, Williams had just three carries that went for more than 20 yards. Corum had five after the Rams Week 8 bye, along with five of his six touchdowns, on the way to a higher yards-per-carry average for the season. 

Corum's one minor injury to Williams away from having the carry split tilted his way for the season, and between his explosiveness and the Rams' penchant for handing it off at the goal line, Corum scoring more than 10 touchdowns isn't out of the question.

Bet: Blake Corum: 10-plus TDs (+500, DraftKings)

New Orleans Saints

The longest shot of the year is reliant on the ball-knowers on the Protector of the Year panel, made up of former offensive linemen. 

It might be a chicken-and-egg thing, but if Kellen Moore and Tyler Shough can take the Saints up a notch from 238.4 passing yards per game and 10 touchdowns in 10 starts, that could either bring attention to the rest of the offense — including the line, or maybe good O-line play would be the reason for a possible leap? Especially since Shough was sacked 31 times in his 10 games last season. 

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

Either way, Erik McCoy returns after missing most of 2025, but, before getting hurt, he had the best pass-blocking grade among all centers, according to PFF. And that was one season after having the best overall grade in 2024, and ranking fifth in 2023. 

It's the longest shot of our 32 bets, but McCoy's been good enough for long enough that he could be the recognized MVP on an improved offense.

Bet: Erik McCoy to win Protector of the Year (175-1, Bet365)

New York Giants 

The Giants would love Jaxson Dart to go against his admirable instincts and get down, or out of bounds, when he scrambles, but we'd be remiss not to note that he's more of an injury candidate than most others at his position. That's why the Giants have Jameis Winston, just in case. 

Even when healthy, Dart averaged just 189.3 passing yards per game in his rookie season. If he managed to play all 17 games this season, that would just barely crawl over his yardage total. 

With the hope for Malik Nabers to be running at full speed early, the assumption that the New York's offense is going to take off with John Harbaugh as head coach and Matt Nagy as offensive coordinator this season seems overly optimistic.

If Dart misses so much as one game, he'll need to average 200 passing yards in the other 16 games, and a 15-game season would require 210 YPG. That's more than Lamar Jackson, Jalen Hurts, Aaron Rodgers, Bryce Young, Cam Ward and several other veteran quarterbacks managed last season. 

Bet: Jaxson Dart under 3,150.5 passing yards (-115, DraftKings)

Philadelphia Eagles

Given his talent level and the defense he plays on, if Jalen Carter is never at least in contention for Defensive Player of the Year, we're going to feel like Ben Affleck's character, at the construction site, telling Matt Damon's Will Hunting what a waste it would be if he never fullfils the promise of his God-given ability, 

The favorite, Myles Garrett, is now with the Rams, which actually hurts his candidacy, as voters may be less likely to reward the result of an obviously stacked defensive line, making this award category more wide open than many think.

Bet: Jalen Carter to win Defensive Player of the Year (25-1)

San Francisco 49ers

As part of the 49ers' efforts to bleed as much as they can out of the end of their once-great core's careers, they added the once-great Mike Evans to a receiving corps that has the betting market expecting something from the long-time Buccaneer. 

I'm expecting relatively little. 

With 11 straight seasons of at laest 1,000 receiving yards to start his career, Evans was once reliable to hit that milestone. If that's why he's lined into the 800s after a season where he played eight games and had 368 yards, then that's an opportunity to fade a future Hall-of-Famer who's further down the road than any of the Niners one might worry about getting hurt this season, and already suffering from a soft tissue (groin) injury. 

Bet: Mike Evans under 824.5 receiving yards (-110, DraftKings)

Seattle Seahawks 

It's the NFC version of a Defensive Player of the Year long-shot bet we made in the AFC edition, as we look at another dominant cornerback on a highly regarded defense. 

Devon Witherspoon is used in a variety of ways by the Seahawks, adding a Super Bowl sack to his résumé as a top cover-corner and one of the best tacklers at the position as well. 

Seattle was a surprise contender through much of last season, but with voters ready to respect its defense this season, and the sheer number of pass-rushers splitting the impact of the defensive front, if the ball finds Witherspoon for a couple of extra splash plays, he'll get attention for DPOY. 

Bet: Devon Witherspoon to win Defensive Player of the Year (+5500, FanDuel)

Tampa Bay Buccaneers

As an exercise, draw a line on the oddsboard where you think the cut off is for teams that are capable of winning the NFC. Last season, you likely would have drawn that line north of the Seahawks. 

This year, you can hit the 10th choice and still just be getting to a favorite for a division, which means the market is not just down on Tampa Bay, but it doesn't think much of the other three teams in the NFC South.

Baker Mayfield, a healthier skill-position group with better defined roles and a top-tier offensive line can take advantage of the other three teams in the division, on the way to stretching last season's 8-2 start to something similar over 17 games — especially if Todd Bowles' defensive youth movement works better than expected. 

A high playoff seed is just as possible as what Seattle accomplished last season, making it worth the long-shot price on a team with as good a path as any to the Super Bowl.

Bet: Buccaneers to win NFC (22-1, DraftKings)

Washington Commanders

Simply put, now that Laremy Tunsil is out for an extended period of time, the Commanders offensive line isn't going to be able to protect Jayden Daniels, and there's no reason to believe last year's poor defense will be transformed by the addition of Sonny Styles, a rookie inside linebacker. 

Against a schedule that is more difficult than it appears at first blush, getting to a Week 11 Monday-nighter at home against the Bengals at 4-5 would be an accomplishment. Even then, Washington would need to split its final eight games, which include Houston, at Minnesota, at Jacksonville, and at Dallas, after that prime-time tilt with Cincinnati.

Bet: Commanders under 7.5 wins (-125, DraftKings)

The 2026-27 NFL season is finally upon us and there are more betting options available than ever at legal sportsbooks, from Super Bowl to MVP to season win totals. Our panel of experts — Michael Fiddle, Matt Jacob, Jeremy Pond and Matt Russell — will be contributing all season to our Yahoo Sports betting coverage.

Now is a perfect time to catch up on all of our preseason NFL betting content, but if you haven't and need a shortened version, here are their favorite futures wagers heading into the season.

Trey Hendrickson to win Defensive Player of The Year (25-1)

Fiddle: This offseason, the Ravens added edge rusher Trey Hendrickson and hired former Los Angelers Chargers defensive coordinator Jesse Minter as head coach. Minter will still call the defensive plays. Defensive linemen and edge rushers in Minter-led defenses have always improved compared with their pass-rushing success rate on previous teams.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

Hendrickson should get to the quarterback more often and could pile up a lot of sacks. Add in Baltimore's early-season schedule, including a Week 1 trip to face the Colts and Daniel Jones coming off Achilles surgery, and this is a no-brainer long-shot preseason award to target.

The lead candidates for this award all have stiffer competition out of the gate. Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald limit one another's ceiling numbers and play the 49ers. Denver Broncos DB Patrick Surtain II is playing Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs in Week 1. The Houston Texans' duo of edge rushers are playing Josh Allen & Co. in Week 1. I like both targeting Hendrickson and fading some of the shorter odds players as well.

Kenneth Walker over 950.5 rushing yards (-114 at FanDuel)

Pond: The biggest personnel issue Kansas City needed to address in the offseason after a 6-11 campaign was at running back.

Well, the Chiefs immediately solved that problem when free agency opened and landed Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker. Gone are Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt from a mediocre backfield; in comes Walker, who will be the featured, three-down back for head coach Andy Reid.

I was high on Walker heading into Seattle's postseason run to the Super Bowl triumph, then grew even more optimistic about his chances to shine when Zach Charbonnet was lost for the season with a torn ACL in the Seahawks' playoff win against San Francisco.

As expected, Walker carried Seattle in style. He ran for more than 300 yards and four touchdowns, including a 49-yard romp into the end zone in the Seahawks' Super Bowl victory against the New England Patriots.

This will mark the 10th season Mahomes will lead the Chiefs under center and he will finally enjoy something that hasn't happened since the two-time NFL MVP took the offensive reins: have a 1,000-yard rusher.

Walker has rushed for at least 1,000 yards twice so far in his career, and he should help lead the Kansas City offense into a deep postseason run.

Dak Prescott over 3,950.5 passing yards (-114 at FanDuel)

Pond: Since 2009, the Cowboys have made the playoffs only seven times, with their most recent trip coming in the 2023 campaign.

Yet, while Dallas has been generally disappointing to its fan base, Dak Prescott hasn't had trouble putting up big numbers through the air during his career. I expect we're going to see big things from Prescott again, as the Cowboys look to end their latest postseason drought.

The only thing that could keep Prescott from eclipsing this number is his health. Over the past seven seasons, Prescott has missed large chunks of three of them. Since 2019, the quarterback's healthy-to-injured seasons have happened every other campaign and — you guessed it — he's coming off a season in which he started all 17 games.

In those four healthy seasons, Prescott tore it up. He passed for 4,902, 4,409, 4,516 and — most recently — 4,552 yards last season.

As for this year's Cowboys, the offense should once again be one of the most electric in the league. Dallas finished fourth in total points (571) a season ago, sitting just behind the Los Angeles Rams, Seattle and Detroit.

Prescott has marque WR duo CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, arguably the best 1-2 combo behind Cincinnati's Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, at his disposal again. Throw in running back Javonte Williams (134 receptions combined in his past three seasons between time spent in Denver and Dallas) and an array of sure-handed tight ends, led by Jake Ferguson, and you have a potent group primed for another stellar offensive campaign. 

I find it extremely difficult to imagine Prescott won't wind up somewhere in the neighborhood of 4,300-4,500 yards passing come season's end.

Carnell Tate under 775.5 receiving yards (-114, FanDuel)

Russell: As humans, we're wired to root for human achievement, but when it comes to season-long player props in the NFL, the under is often the better play, especially for a rookie receiver whose selection early in April's NFL draft was met with something like, "Oh … really?"

When the Titans picked Jeremiah Smith's Ohio State teammate, Carnell Tate, the teams behind them were delighted to get a defender falling in their lap. That doesn't mean Tate can't be great, but we can only go off of his in-game performances almost anytime the Buckeyes played an adequate defense from a team with anywhere near their talent. 

Last season, Tate had just 12 total receptions in games against Texas, Washington, Indiana and Miami — and in 2024, he had 11 total catches against Oregon (twice), Penn State, Indiana, Tennessee and Notre Dame.

Of the 33 quarterbacks to get 200-plus snaps during a game-state where neither team had a win probability of 80% or higher, Cam Ward was 32nd in EPA/Play (Expected Points Added/Play) and 31st in CPOE (Completion Percentage Over Expected). 

Tate can have success when players around him are putting him in a better situation to succeed, but not the other way around. With Elic Ayomanor a year ahead of him, and Calvin Ridley likely to get Ward's first read on most plays, Tate is likely to struggle against pro defensive backs — the kind he would have seen against the college teams listed above.

Denver Broncos under 9.5 wins (+110)

Jacob: Momentum is a massive intangible in the NFL. So, too, is the schedule and how it sets up. Not exactly breaking news, I know — but the obvious is worth stating in reference to the Denver Broncos' 2026 win total.

Last year, on the way to going 14-3 and capturing the AFC's No. 1 seed, the Broncos gained steam while taking advantage of a highly favorable schedule.

After knocking off the lowly Titans in Week 1, Denver suffered consecutive losses to the Colts (road) and Chargers (home) by a combined four points.

From there, the Broncos went 13-1. They won nine games against teams that were on vacation by mid-January (Chiefs twice, Raiders twice, Bengals, Jets, Giants, Cowboys and Commanders), and two against opponents that lost their only playoff game (Chargers and Eagles).

Denver also defeated Houston (1-1 in the postseason) and lost to Jacksonville (another one-and-done playoff entrant).

In other words, the NFL schedule makers did the Broncos a solid last year. Spoiler alert: It won't be a cakewalk in 2026.

After opening in Kansas City, Denver faces — in order — Jacksonville (home), the Rams (home), San Francisco (road), the Chargers (road) and Seattle (home). Good luck building early-season momentum.

Things ease up from there, with trips to Arizona, Carolina, Pittsburgh, Las Vegas and the Jets interspersed with home games against Kansas City, Las Vegas and Miami. But the finishing stretch is no joke: Buffalo (home), New England (road), the Chargers (home).

Will Denver again field an elite defense? Absolutely. Will quarterback Bo Nix make more strides in his third year with coach Sean Payton? Probably.

Will it translate in the win-loss column like it did last fall? Doubtful.

item.title: Mike Tomlin chooses Josh Allen as the quarterback he would love to coach: 'He's built for it'
item.description: Mike Tomlin is a big fan of the Bills' star quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
After 19 seasons, Mike Tomlin decided to step away from the Pittsburgh Steelers. He'll spend the 2026 NFL season as an analyst instead.

But given Tomlin's success in the NFL — and the fact that he didn't retire — rumors are going to pop up any time a high-profile job becomes available. While Tomlin appears happy with his new role, he did reveal the one young quarterback he would love to coach right now.

No, it's not Joe Burrow or Lamar Jackson, two quarterbacks he saw a lot of when he was with the Steelers. It's Buffalo Bills star Josh Allen, who Tomlin said is "built for this" during an appearance on the PFF NFL Show.

"Who do I wanna coach? I'd take Josh Allen." - Mike Tomlin has vehement praise for the Bills QB1 😤 | @JacCollinsworthpic.twitter.com/LC7lqvczD3

— PFF (@PFF) September 8, 2026

Other than Allen's age — he's 30 — it's tough to argue with Tomlin's choice. Over the past six seasons, Allen has emerged as arguably the best quarterback in football. He's been a strong MVP candidate in five of those seasons, pulling off an MVP win in 2024. As Tomlin explained, Allen can get it done with his arm or his legs, and is among the best dual threats in the league as well.

Whether Tomlin actually gets a chance to coach Allen, however, seems pretty unlikely. While Tomlin stepped away from the Steelers, the head coach is reportedly still under contract with the team. He can't simply put his name in the hat if the Bills' job suddenly becomes available. The Steelers — which still hold Tomlin's coaching rights — would have to trade him away.

The Bills, meanwhile, likely aren't in the market for a new head coach in the next couple seasons. After surprisingly firing Sean McDermott in January, the team decided to hire Joe Brady as its next head coach. Brady will presumably get a few seasons in the role before the team moves on … unless things really collapse under his leadership.

Assuming Brady gets multiple years on the job, Tomlin wouldn't have a realistic shot to coach Allen until the quarterback was no longer considered "young" for his position. Tomlin recognized he was stretching the definition of a young quarterback by choosing Allen, who's already been in the NFL for eight seasons.

Whenever Tomlin decides to get back into coaching, he should draw plenty of interest from other NFL teams. Tomlin famously never posted a losing season with the Steelers, and a number of other NFL franchises would kill for that kind of consistency right now.

For now, Tomlin has the luxury of being able to wait on a premier job to open up before he returns. It might not be with the Bills, but Tomlin will almost certainly put himself in position to excel right away in his next head-coaching role.
