item.title: Bills must be prepared for this unique but straight-forward wrinkle from Texans defense
item.description: The Bills have to be prepared for this against the Texans defense
item.content:encoded:
The Houston Texans aren’t an exotic defense. They don’t utilize creativity get to the quarterback on a regular basis. It’s probably the NFL’s most straight-forward, pin-your-ears-back defensive scheme.

That is not to say the Bills can scrap the gameplanning portion of this week for what their offense will see across the line of scrimmage on a play-to-play basis in Week 1. It’s to suggest their strategy for attacking Houston’s vaunted defense needs to be anchored in not expecting extra rushers being sent toward Josh Allen.

Last season, the Texans had the lowest blitz rate in all of football, at just 16.7%, yet finished seventh with a pressure rate of 40.3%, per Fantasy Points Data — a dream scenario for any defensive coordinator.

That combination was integral to that unit’s excellence. And Houston was able to essentially duplicate those magical percentages in the game against the Bills in Week 12 last year.

In that victory, the Texans blitzed Allen on just 15.2% of his 39 drop backs and still managed to pressure him 43.5% of the time. Seven of his eight sacks came without a blitz! That has to be exceptionally rare in the NFL.

And check the difference for Allen in that game, split by when he was blitzed and not blitzed.

Of course, Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins were dinged in that contest. The former toughed it out but clearly was not himself, and Dawkins left the game for a long stretch, which led to 17 relief-appearance snaps for Ryan Van Demark. Dalton Kincaid didn’t play due to that knee injury. There was no Keon Coleman.

Also, Allen dropped back to pass on 28 of 39 plays in the second half, an aerial-centric attack I’d normally advocate for, but such telegraphing in that particular game felt far from ideal. Heck, Joe Brady even admitted to a less-than-stellar play-calling job after the defeat.

But it’s not as though Allen — and Brady — regularly struggled against teams that played coverage against the Bills offense and held back on blitzing. Even with this Week 12 performance included, Allen’s 105.4 quarterback rating against no-blitz plays from opposing defenses ranked third-best in the entire NFL among qualifying passers.

If that game is removed, that rating jumped to 110.4, quite naturally.

As a longtime Bills pass-game pusher, particularly due to Allen’s presence, it’s somewhat unorthodox for me to advocate for the run game. Then again, it’s not lost on me that James Cook is the league’s reigning rushing champion, and in the first half of that Week 12 outing a season ago, he had 71 yards on seven carries including a 45-yard touchdown run.

More Cook in this game — probably a smart idea for the Bills, because he’s clearly one of the league’s most explosive offensive weapons, and his continued usage keeps Houston’s pass rush honest. Limiting the Texans duo of Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter is, of course, vital to beating this AFC South team.

Buffalo has preached the “they have to play us” mentality all offseason, and playing the Bills is dealing with Allen, his assembly of pass catchers… and Cook.

We’ll see if Brady learned his lesson schematically from last year’s contest.

How do you think the Bills should handle the Texans minimal-blitzing defense?

item.title: 2026 NFL predictions: Detroit Lions defensive MVP
item.description: Our staff makes their 2026 NFL predictions for Detroit Lions defensive MVP. Don’t forget to vote!
item.content:encoded:
While the Detroit Lions’ offense is filled with proven talent, the defensive side of the ball has a few more questions than answers. That said, there is still some top end talent. In total, five Lions defenders have earned All Pro or Pro Bowl honors: Aidan Hutchinson, Jack Campbell, Devin White, Brian Branch, and Kerby Joseph. That’s actually the exact same number as the defense (Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta, Penei Sewell).

So, maybe there are more candidates for the 2026 Detroit Lions defensive MVP than you think.

As we continue our 2026 NFL predictions, here are our picks for Lions 2026 defensive MVP. Don’t forget to cast your vote at the bottom of the page!

Previously:

  • Offensive MVP predictions

Who will be the Lions’ defensive MVP in 2026?

Morgan Cannon: Jack Campbel

Obviously, there is an argument to be made for the monster on the edge that wears #97, but I am going with Campbell because I think by end of season, he will be the unquestioned heartbeat of the defense. From racking up tackles, forcing fumbles, and being a general game-wrecker against opposing team’s running games, he is also a seasoned veteran in defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard’s defense. Being able to ensure everyone is where they need to be, while also being in control of pre-snap checks and shifts is going to pay huge dividends for the Lions in 2026.

Al Karsten: Alim McNeill

It hasn’t exactly been a fairytale 20-plus months for Alim McNeill since tearing his ACL in Week 15 of 2024, just two months after signing his blockbuster contract extension. But for the hip-hop artist who goes by “Dream,” the nightmare appears to be over—and his dreams are very much at the forefront of reality after a remarkably strong bounceback during Lions training camp.

While the expectation is for Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell to continue their All-Pro-level play, McNeill has an opportunity to completely shapeshift this defense if he can consistently maximize his talents. If the version of McNeill who flashed from 2022-24 returns for a career year, Detroit suddenly has the makings of a lethal defensive front capable of helping propel this unit into the top 10.

Like his draft classmate Milton Williams did for the Patriots after joining them last offseason, McNeill could provide the type of uplifting impact that helps spearhead a defense on a run to the Super Bowl. A season with 7+ sacks, 20+ quarterback hits, and 10+ tackles for loss would make Detroit a force to be reckoned with come January and February.

Erik Schlitt: Aidan Hutchinson

The Lions’ defensive line looked great in training camp and could be a huge catalyst in their defensive success. Hutchinson is already one of the best defensive players in the NFL, but with a healthy Alim McNeill, improved Tyleik Williams, along with DJ Wonnum and Derrick Moore splitting time on the opposite edge, Hutchinson should see his opportunities increase and could be in for a monster season.

Jeremy Reisman: Aidan Hutchinson

I believe Hutchinson is in for a career year. While I think his supporting cast is better, I don’t think that will draw any attention away from Hutch. But with some of the things we’ve seen in training camp, I don’t believe defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is just going to let teams add an extra tight end or running back to Hutchinson’s side and make him fight off double and triple teams every play. No, the Lions are committed to keeping their pass rush creative this year, and Hutchinson is going to EAT.

John Whiticar: Jack Campbell

In the past, Aidan Hutchinson was the clear-cut MVP on defense, but Campbell has now become 1B to his 1A. However, I think the Lions have added a lot of good defenders to pair with Hutchinson (Wonnum, Moore, Gill-Howard) and with Alim McNeill back and healthy, Hutchinson will no longer be leaned on as the only reliable lineman on the roster. Campbell, meanwhile, is far and away the Lions’ best linebacker, a position that is vital to every part of the defense.

Ryan Mathews: Aidan Hutchinson

Aidan Hutchinson will be the Lions’ defensive MVP in 2026. This is as talented and deep the defensive line has been in Detroit since Hutchinson arrived in 2022. And while Hutchinson will be a key part of gameplanning for any opposing offensive coordinator, there’s going to be plenty of chances for Hutchinson to make impact plays.

Anthony Balaj: Brian Branch

While Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson will likely be tapped with the All-Pro accolades, Branch will be the player that unlocks Kelvin Sheppard’s ability to dynamically disguise the defensive scheme (and likely land Sheppard a head coaching job in 2027).

Brandon Knapp: Aidan Hutchinson

While he was looking to be on a career season in 2024, that injury didn’t appear to slow him down as much in 2025. Now that he’s had a full year under his belt post-injury, and more help added to the opposite EDGE position and the interior defensive line, I think Hutchinson makes a true case for DPOY in 2026. The help fans have pleaded for has arrived, and I think Hutchinson will benefit the most out of it.

item.title: Chiefs begin week as favorites over the Broncos in Week 1
item.description: Kansas City enters Week 1 as a 2.5-point favorite in an AFC West battle with Denver.
item.content:encoded:
To cap off Week 1 of the NFL season, on Monday evening, the Kansas City Chiefs will host the Denver Broncos for a “Monday Night Football” bout at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri. Kickoff is scheduled for 7:15 p.m. The game will be broadcast nationally on ABC and ESPN.

According to FanDuel Sportsbook, Kansas City begins the week as a 2.5-point favorite.

The last time these two franchises faced off was Christmas Day at Arrowhead; Denver closed as a 13.5-point favorite against the Chiefs without quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Kansas City covered, but the Broncos pulled away from a tie game in the fourth quarter to win 20-13.

Of course, Denver’s victory sealed the clean sweep of the Chiefs in 2025: in Week 11, the Chiefs were four-point favorites on the road against the Broncos, but lost 22-19.

In the 2026 preseason, the Chiefs were defeated by the Los Angeles Rams, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Seattle Seahawks. The Broncos beat the Atlanta Falcons and Minnesota Vikings, but lost to the Green Bay Packers.

item.title: Cutting Darius Slayton is a move the Giants might regret
item.description: With a lot of question marks at wide receiver, the Giants still rolled the dice by letting Slayton go.
item.content:encoded:
John Harbaugh is running a meritocracy, and Darius Slayton’s play this summer did not warrant him being ahead of any other wide receiver on the New York Giants’ roster. That is the biggest reason Slayton is an ex-Giant today.

Slayton missed the entire spring after double sports hernia surgery. He had a quiet summer, admitting not long ago that he still was not running at 100%, though he felt “pretty good.” Malik Nabers is the Giants’ No. 1 wide receiver. Malachi Fields, Odell Beckham Jr., and Darnell Mooney were all better than Slayton this summer. For that matter, practice squad receivers Braxton Berrios and Dalen Cambre were also better.

Slayton was ticketed for the game-day inactive list when Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys rolled around.

None of that means that cutting Slayton isn’t a massive gamble by the Giants.

The Giants have already lost one wide receiver they were going to count on heavily, Calvin Austin, to a season-ending injury. Depth at the position is now, to use an informal word, sketchy.

Yes, moving on from Slayton is likely a sign that the Giants feel good about the possibility that Nabers will play Sunday against the Cowboys. Even if he plays, though, Nabers will probably play a limited number of snaps in his return from last season’s torn ACL.

Fields is a rookie third-round pick. He had an impressive summer, but there is no guarantee he can carry that performance into real games. We have seen impressive summers fizzle before when fall arrived.

Beckham earned his spot, no doubt. Still, he is a 33-year-old who did not play in 2025 and has not played a full NFL season since 2019 — yes, 2019. How much can he play? How long before his body breaks down and he misses time? How productive can he be when he does play?

Darnell Mooney has a 1,000-yard and a 900-yard receiving season on his resume over six NFL seasons. He is coming off a down year with the Atlanta Falcons, though, where he caught just 32 passes for 443 yards. Are the Giants going to get a version of Mooney that deserves consistent playing time?

What about the practice squad guys?

Berrios has six receptions in 10 games over the past two seasons. Cambre was impressive this summer, but he has played 16 NFL offensive snaps and does not have a catch. Jalin Hyatt? Thirteen receptions over the past two seasons. Charlie Jones has eight catches in 33 career games, only one of which came in the last two seasons.

Can any of them produce at an acceptable level if the Giants need them to play extended snaps at wide receiver? That is debatable.

Slayton hate is unwarranted

The subhead says exactly what it is meant to say. Slayton has been a better player than many Giants fans, needing someone or something to blame for the struggles of recent seasons, are willing to admit.

Yes, his career drop rate of 6.3% is too high. No, he was never able to be what the Giants needed in the pre-Nabers days — a bona fide No. 1 receiver.

Let’s be real, though.

Slayton was a fifth-round pick, 171st overall, out of Auburn in the 2019 NFL Draft. He has not been an All-Pro like 2023 fifth-round pick Puka Nacua, but Slayton has vastly outplayed his draft position.

Slayton led the Giants in receiving yards four times in seven seasons, with 700+ receiving yards in each of those seasons. He has a 15.0 yards-per-catch average. He is four catches shy of 300 for his career, and his 4,435 receiving yards are 565 short of 5,000.

Slayton is 14th on the team’s all-time receptions list. His career average is 42 receptions per season. If he accomplished that in 2026, he would have moved all the way to ninth.

Slayton is 12th on the team’s all-time list in receiving yards. His average 633-yard receiving season would have skyrocketed him to fifth, behind only Amani Toomer, Odell Beckham Jr., Frank Gifford, and Tiki Barber.

Slayton has been a good player for the Giants. Instead of ripping him for his shortcomings and pointing a finger at him as part of the reason the team has been mostly awful during his time in New York, fans should be thanking him for being an overachiever, a good player, and an excellent representative of the franchise during his time with it.

We have seen Slayton outplay expectations before. There might come a time this season when the Giants wish they still had him around to try and do it again.

item.title: Jumbo Package: Keelon Russell and Alabama may be working their way back to the top ten
item.description: It was an encouraging opening week for the Tide, but there’s a long ways to go
item.content:encoded:
We’re going heavy on the video links today. First up, we got press conferences from the whole contingent of Alabama coaches.

Will Sanders got the start, but Mal Waldrep got more snaps.

Alabama offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb provided some clarity on the situation Monday.

“Will was dealing with a little bit of an oblique, and so trying to help him out to get through the game, he had battled through it all week, and he’s doing great now,” Grubb said. “But we knew we had a guy now that had taken a lot of reps with the ones all camp. So I felt good about getting both those guys out there and getting reps. Certainly would’ve loved to see Will finish out the game. He came back out there. But we’d like to keep the lineup as consistent as possible.”

I felt like Sanders had a bit of a rough go at things, an an oblique injury would definitely explain that.

I don’t really have an opinion in the battle between Sanders and Waldrep, but I do hope one of the two really steps up and takes over. It seems like Grubb does as well, as that was his message here. Which really makes you wonder just how we got to where we got last season with the line rotating all season long.

Luke has really taken great ownership of the way we’re supposed to communicate as a linebacking corps. I think he had great leadership in that from Deontae Lawson and Nikhai Hill-Green when he was here. I think he’s taken that to another level, and Chuck Morrell has done a fantastic job with those guys. We talk about the way we communicate as a linebacking corps needs to be demonstrative; that is intimidating to the other side of the ball when you communicate like that. Then we want to play the game with anticipation, so there are a lot of keys and indicators that we get those linebackers clued into that they, as individuals, have to communicate that on the field. Luke did a fantastic job of that; Caleb does a really good job of that as well. So from an effort standpoint, from a communication standpoint, I thought that linebacking corps had a nice first outing.”

I thought this was an interesting comment, and not one that I think I had heard from a coach before. Wommack mentions that he wants pre-snap communication to be demonstrative because it can be intimidating to the other team. And I think I agree with that, seen an opposing defense constantly barking out communications definitely gives a air of put-togetherness that may be a little disconcerting. So I like that it’s something Wommack is thinking about and emphasizing. It’s a small thing, but it’s an edge.

Three injured Alabama players, Jireh Edwards, AK Dear and Noah Rogers, participated in pregame warmups before Saturday’s season opener against East Carolina but did not play in the Crimson Tide’s dominant 48-10 victory.

While none of the three were ready to return against the Pirates, their participation in warmups was an encouraging sign.

According to DeBoer, two of the three injured players could be particularly close to returning.

Sounds like Jireh Edwards and AK Dear are close to getting back. I’m not totally sure where Dear fits into things at this point – Hill, Crowell, and Brown look like a really nice trio of running backs. Still, he’s definitely a talented player that will be good to have back.

Jireh Edwards is also a guy that I think could factor in quite a bit this season as a sub-package player that can act as a dime linebacker to bring some size to formations that are heavy on the DBs.

TIGHT END

Kaleb Edwards: 56 snaps (67.5%)
Marshall Pritchett: 34 snaps (41%)
Josh Ford: 19 snaps (22.9%)
Danny Lewis: 12 snaps (14.5%)
Jay Lindsey: 9 snaps (10.8%)

OBSERVATIONS: Speaking of the tight ends, how about that rotation? Five different guys got meaningful action on Saturday. We had wondered if Alabama would use four guys after the return of Danny Lewis, and we were still too light on those predictions. That’s a good thing though, especially when you watched how these guys performed against East Carolina.

Marshall Pritchett got the start alongside Kaleb Edwards, as the Crimson Tide started the game in 12 personnel. The package isn’t surprising considering all the practice clips and nuggets we received about the strength of this room, but I was still a little surprised that Pritchett got the nod over Josh Ford despite him being listed as the starter at the H.

Josh Ford being well behind Edwards and Pritchett was surprising to me. A month ago, I expected Ford and Edwards to be the main two. Over fall camp, it did seem like Pritchett had worked his way in, and I was expecting about a 3-way split between those guys. Instead, it seemed like Edwards is the clear #1, Pritchett is the #2, and Ford is the role player.

And even then, Jay Lindsey came in to play fullback on the goal line, which is also something I was expecting they would use Ford for.

I still think this group could be the key to making or breaking Alabama’s season, much more than many people give them credit for. If they can shore up the perimeter blocking compared to last year, it’ll be a huge improvement for the offense. On top of that, I think the WR group is going to be pared down a bit compared to last year, so they could be needed more in the passing game.

Alabama

To Make CFP: +134
Title Odds: +2500

I have my questions about the Tide this season, but against overmatched ECU, Bama had little trouble. It was 38-10 at halftime and Keelon Russell accounted for 342 yards (86 rushing). Two conference games and a visit from Florida State await and that’s when we’ll continue to learn if this season will be a special one in Tuscaloosa.

I’m going to be honest, I don’t know who this Chris Fallica guy is or why we should care. He writes for Fox Sports? Anyway, he’s like the only national pundit I’ve seen go ahead and move Alabama into the top ten. Cool!

Week 1 of any college football season is never short on overreactions, and that holds especially true when one of the sport’s biggest blue blood programs introduces a new starting quarterback.

Such was the case for Alabama Crimson Tide, ranked No. 11 in the preseason US LBM Coaches Poll, under a sweltering heat inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa on Saturday as folks got their first glances of former five-star quarterback Keelon Russell playing meaningful snaps.

Russell’s first career start saw him account for 342 all-purpose yards in a 48-10 victory over East Carolina. The recruiting industry’s No. 2-ranked quarterback in the class of 2025 completed 18 of his 30 passes for 256 yards and rushed for 86 yards and a touchdown on 13 attempts.

Which of those two stats was more impressive depends on who you ask, but it was the type of performance Russell needed. He may not have been perfect, but he more than showed off the promise, raw talent and sheer athleticism that won him the starting quarterback job over experienced senior Austin Mack in fall camp.

Roll Tide Wire put together a compilation of national pundits talking about Keelon Russell. Seems like most out there took notice and are pretty bullish on him. Interestingly, this one feels like the national people may be higher on Russell than a lot of Bama fans after the game, who have been grumbling a bit about how long he held the ball and the bout of inaccuracy in the 3rd quarter.

Finally, here’s the SEC Shorts this week. Enjoy!

item.title: Five NFL teams that could race to strong starts in 2026 season
item.description: A September surge isn't always indicative of a team's full-season performance, but these five NFL teams could be poised to start strong this season.
item.content:encoded:
A strong start to the season can set NFL teams on the right foot toward a long, deliberate march toward the playoffs – or provide a full-on illusion.

Figuring out what to make of a good early impression can be difficult, with any given team's long-term viability often not coming into focus until far deeper into the fall. Still, there's no questioning that coaches covet building an initial advantage in the standings rather than falling into a hole. With fortuitous schedules and the components to click in the opening weeks, several organizations are on track to pull ahead of their competition in the first month or two.

Here are five NFL teams that could be poised to start the new season strong with an early-season run:

Detroit Lions

Last season's crash landing to the bottom of the NFC North standings was a particularly painful outcome for a franchise that had already begun to question how long its competitive window would remain ajar. It did, however, confer one major benefit: a schedule that some might view as the league's softest setup.

If Detroit can emerge unblemished after its Week 2 prime-time showdown with the Bills, there's a solid chance for the organization to secure just its second 5-0 start in the Super Bowl era. Prior to the Week 6 bye, that contest in Buffalo will be the lone one against a team that had a winning record last season.

With a new offensive coordinator in Drew Petzing and a reshuffled offensive line counting on several young starters to step up in short order, the Lions might seem like an odd candidate to find their footing right away. But last year's offense, which finished fourth in scoring, proved that it still has plenty of firepower even when it lacks the consistency Petzing was hired to weave into the attack. The more troublesome vulnerability might be in a secondary that figures to be without safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph for a while, but few teams on the early schedule beyond the Bills look capable of exploiting that weakness.

Pittsburgh Steelers

Embracing change isn't exactly a strong suit for a franchise that has been the NFL's foremost example of staying the course. Yet even with a new day thrust upon it by Mike Tomlin's resignation, Pittsburgh looks positioned to weather any turbulence brought about by the transition to new coach Mike McCarthy.

A bespoke offense figures to keep Aaron Rodgers well within his comfort zone, regardless of how much of a limitation that configuration later proves to be. So long as extension negotiations with cornerback Joey Porter Jr. don't reach a boiling point, the league's highest-paid defense could be invigorated by defensive coordinator Patrick Graham's new scheme, which figures to be far more dynamic than the long static approach that bordered on becoming stale. And while the staying power of a roster that ranked as the NFL's oldest after cutdown day could become a concern down the stretch, the Steelers should stand to benefit out of the gate from an experience advantage.

The real boon, however, is the schedule configuration. Prior to its Week 9 bye, Pittsburgh will have just one major test in a Week 2 showdown with the Patriots. Beyond that, the first half of the season doesn't feature any games against teams that had a winning record last year.

Dallas Cowboys

A year ago, Dallas was navigating a good deal of uncertainty as it began its inaugural season under first-time head coach Brian Schottenheimer. Now, the Cowboys have all the vital pieces back in place for one of the league's most electric offenses, which still has room to level up thanks to the continuity that could be unlocked in Year 2 of the system.

The obvious area of concern, however, is last year's dilapidated defense, which might remain a grab bag after undergoing a massive offseason overhaul under new defensive coordinator Christian Parker. But the Vic Fangio protege figures to significantly enhance the diversity of coverage looks, which will no doubt aid a secondary defined by its frequent short-circuiting. Between the expected Fangio-esque boost in the schematic safeguards against deep passes and clearer communication on the back end, there's a clear path to significant improvement for the defense – even if that only leads to somewhere near the middle of the pack at first.

Dallas also stands to benefit from a September schedule that will bring matchups against three teams sorting out significant shifts: the Giants, Commanders and Ravens. The loss of three-time Pro Bowl left guard Tyler Smith for several weeks is a notable hit to the team's stability quotient, but his absence might not be much of an impediment until contests with the Texans and Buccaneers in Weeks 4-5. Still, this is a rare start to build some confidence in the early going for a franchise that has had just one 3-0 start (2019) since 2009.

San Francisco 49ers

For a franchise that has almost annually been without peer in its injury misfortune, the 49ers largely seem to be trending in the right direction with their most critical contributors. Defensive end Nick Bosa is set to play in the season opener in Australia against the Rams, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said. And just eight months removed from tearing his Achilles, tight end George Kittle appears likely to follow suit.

That's not to say that San Francisco won't be operating at a significant personnel deficit against its loaded rival. The outlook at receiver is still tenuous, as is the depth at defensive end with Mykel Williams remaining on the physically unable to perform list to open the season. Still, no one understands how to push forward while shorthanded quite like Kyle Shanahan does. His deeply rooted system and singular play-calling acumen should enable the offense to get up to speed far faster than competitors who are at much closer to full strength.

After the opener down under, the 49ers could be primed to go on a run. A three-game home stand follows, with meetings against the Dolphins and Cardinals likely serving as mere tune-ups. The stretch entering midseason is also highly manageable. Tilts against the Commanders and Falcons await before the Week 8 bye, and the Raiders await coming out of it.

MONDAY MORNING JB: Rams vs 49ers chess match starting early – in the air

Baltimore Ravens

There's a good amount of upheaval afoot for Baltimore, which ended John Harbaugh's 18-year run to embrace the unknown with first-time head coach Jesse Minter. Yet even if the Ravens might be more unpredictable than others on this list in establishing an early trajectory, their blemishes could be covered by a forgiving first-half slate.

Through the first seven weeks, the Ravens won't square off against a team that had a winning record in 2025. That stretch also turns up three opponents that finished in last place in their respective divisions. And Baltimore will have to leave home just once in the opening four weeks.

How fast, then, can the team get up to speed given the radical changes on both sides of the ball? If his previous work with the Chargers serves as any indication of what's to come, Minter's defense might not take long to coalesce, thanks in large part to his knack for creating buy-in from players to a detail-focused approach. First-time offensive coordinator Declan Doyle might require a lengthier timeline to find his way as a play-caller, but his expected scheme should suit Lamar Jackson well by catering to his underutilized strength of working the middle of the field.

item.title: 2026 NFL Season Award Predictions: Coach of the Year
item.description: The WCG Crew is predicting the 2026 NFL Awards, and next is our pick for Coach of the Year.
item.content:encoded:
Some of the Windy City Gridiron staff made their picks for several 2026 individual season awards, and we’ll cap the predictions off by picking Super Bowl LXI. We’ve been running through all our picks the last couple of days, and next up is Coach of the Year.

MVP
Offensive Player of the Year
Defensive Player of the Year
Offensive Rookie of the Year
Defensive Rookie of the Year
Coach of the Year

Super Bowl LXI

Bryan Orenchuk: I’m going with Ben Johnson. He wants records broken on offense – we’ll see records broken on offense and one of the most explosive offenses this century as the Chicago Bears firmly establish themselves as contenders under his leadership.

Josh Sunderbruch: I want it to be Johnson, but I think it’s going to be Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers.

Donald Gooch: Ben Johnson probably should have won it last year, but this year he leads the Bears to a second-division win in the toughest division in football, and he cements himself as one of, if not the, top offensive minds in football.

Sam Householder: DeMeco Ryans – The Houston Texans have a very good team, and I think they could break through for a season that turns a lot of heads.

Mongo Peanut: Kyle Shanahan. I think he’s going to go toe-to-toe with McVay and end up winning the division with a more flawed roster. This alone should win him the right.

TJ Starman: Jesse Minter is my choice for coach of the year. I don’t think there’s an obvious team that was in the depths last season that will rise up this year, but Minter should be able to revitalize a talented Baltimore Ravens roster and get the most out of them.

Erik Duerrwaechter: I’d argue Ben Johnson was snubbed last year in his first-ever season as a head coach. In year two, the league will learn to fear and appreciate him for the greatness he’s capable of achieving.

Gary Baugher Jr.: Always the toughest to forecast because usually it goes to a coach who facilitated a turnaround with a bad team. So, of the new hires (or previous coaches who find themselves on new teams), I like the situation John Harbaugh is in. The defense is a top-half unit overall, and if he can unlock Dart more, I can see a 9-10 win season from the Giants with their 4th-place schedule.

Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: Minter will take the Ravens from a sub .500 team back to the playoffs, which is the kind of thing voters look for.

Jeff Berckes: Sometimes this goes to the coach of a purely dominant team, but so often it goes to a coach that exceeds expectations. As if the media wasn’t wrong in their preseason forecast, and it was an amazing coaching job that lifted the team up. The NFC South has the following over/under win expectations: Panthers 6.5, Saints 7.5, Falcons 7.5, and Buccaneers 8.5. Someone has to win this division, and I’d be willing to put a dollar on the Saints emerging and Kellen Moore taking it home.

Superfans: Honestly, the only negative surrounding Ben Johnson is a lack of facial hair, but we think the voters will overlook that and pick him after he leads the Bears to back-to-back NFC North titles.

Albert Breer’s Takeaways: Where Every NFL Team Stands Heading Into the 2026 Season

It’s really rare that a veteran coach such as Dan Quinn goes through the sort of on-the-fly wholesale philosophical change that the Commandersdid this offseason, and there’s no question it’s just different with more complex schemes coming in with new coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones. Mark Tyler breaks down Commanders defense & why it will be the backbone of the 2026 campaign

More than half of the defense has completely turned over. Gone are Von Miller (who was once a great player in this league) and Jacob Martin. They are being replaced by uber-athletic edge rushers in Oweh and Chaisson. Dorance Armstrong, who was a starter last year before being injured, should slot into a rotational role along with rookie Joshua Josephs once he returns from his one-game suspension.

The interior has been bolstered by the additions of Tim Settle and Charles Omehihu to go along with Payne and Kinlaw. Both are scheme/technique diverse and can be moved around the front five.

Washington’s linebacker corps has been completely revamped. Styles takes over for the aging Bobby Wagner – who was a liability anywhere outside the A and B gaps and in coverage. He offers the ability to impact all three levels of this defense and will share green dot responsibilities with veteran Frankie Luvu. Speaking of Luvu, he came into camp in the best shape of his career and is looking to regain his 2024 form after being played out of position for the majority of 2025. Leo Chenal is the new free-agent addition, and his versatility and toughness against the run and as a situational pass rusher as a walked-up SAM will be a welcome addition to this defense.

The Commanders defensive backs have taken on a completely new identity. Safety Nick Cross will be the leader of the secondary. His presence on the defense will force offensive coordinators to monitor his alignment on every play. Jeremy Reaves and Quan Martin (who had a very good training camp), will both see time in Jones’ three-safety looks and Tyler Owens seems to have carved out a role as a “position-less player” who can be deployed at all three levels. Sainristil and Robertson can move between the inside and outside with Douglas and Moreau adding the veteran presences until Trey Amos returns.

Three offensive players I’m watching closely in Week 1 against the Eagles

TE Chig Okonkwo

The former Maryland product is known for creating yards after the catch and has an explosive athletic profile. Built like a wide receiver at 6’3″ and 238 pounds, Okonkwo may not have the precise route-running savvy of Ertz, but he should inject a different kind of vertical stress into the offense.

In D.C., he will be playing with the best quarterback of his career. In Tennessee, his ceiling was capped by a revolving door of shaky quarterback play, and now he has a signal-caller with pinpoint accuracy who can lead him up the field.

Okonkwo signed a three-year, $30M deal this offseason to bring some serious youth and explosiveness to our tight end room. The Commanders desperately lacked a true seam-buster last year, especially as Ertz battled injuries down the stretch. Enter Okonkwo, who is coming off career highs with 56 receptions for 560 yards. More importantly, the man is an absolute YAC monster: last season, he ranked 7th among all NFL tight ends in Yards After Catch per reception at 6.2 yards, according to Next Gen Stats.

We haven’t seen Okonkwo much this offseason due to the team managing his health, but all signs point to a breakout season for the former Titan. Will this come to fruition, or did we all fall for Ashburn Syndrome? I want to see some heavy targets dialed up for Chig right out of the gate in Week 1. In Tennessee, he thrived on manufactured touches—designed bubble screens, motion out of the backfield, and flexing into the slot to isolate linebackers. If the Eagles try to pin their ears back and play aggressive coverage to slow down Terry McLaurin, Okonkwo should find plenty of green grass over the middle for quick, explosive catch-and-run opportunities.

If you’ve been paying attention, there are actually several reasons to be hopeful for a successful season for the Commanders. Diggs is the most recent addition to generate excitement and hope, though, and his signing is one of the most impactful for this team. The Washington Commanders have announced that quarterback Jayden Daniels, wide receiver Terry McLaurin, linebacker Frankie Luvu, safety Jeremy Reaves and punter Tress Way will serve as captains for the 2026 season.

NFL Once Again Pushing Boundaries As New Season Kicks Off

The eve of the 2026 NFL season arrives Tuesday as the league continues to push the boundaries of its popularity both domestically and internationally

This season’s opener—on NBC, as usual—is on Wednesday because the NFL’s debut game in Australia (49ers-Rams) will air Thursday night due to the league’s inability to play on Friday like it has done on Week 1 the previous two years. That’s because the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 precludes pro football games from happening on Fridays or Saturdays beginning with the second Friday of September and continuing through the second Saturday in December. The 49ers-Rams matchup is being played Friday morning in Australia, but that does not violate the rules, since Melbourne is 14 hours ahead of the U.S. East Coast, giving the game an 8:35 p.m. ET kick off.

Wednesday night football will be a theme this year, as the Packers and Rams will play in the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve game, to be streamed exclusively on Netflix. The streamer drew strong viewership for the most recent Wednesday NFL games on Christmas Day in 2024.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Happy Birthday ESPN

A new QB metric from The Athletic

Introducing QB Index: A perfect QB stat everyone will love, and no one will disagree with

What is QBI?

QBI is a forward-looking quarterback efficiency metric that uses play-by-play data, adjusts for context in each play and is opponent-aware. Put more simply, QBI takes into account passes, rushes, scrambles, sacks, turnovers and anything else that happens when the football is in the quarterback’s hands.

But it goes a step deeper and adjusts for whether the quarterback was pressured, if that pressure was quick (less than 2.5 seconds), as well as the quality of the offensive line and receivers. QBI factors in fumbles in an attempt to take the luck out of recoveries — this can work for and against a quarterback depending on who recovered. QBI also takes into account drops by receivers, as well as yards after the catch and uses an expected YAC model to assign or remove credit from the quarterback. Of course, EPA and success rate are factors in the model, as well. There is still value in knowing that a 12-yard completion on third-and-20 is not as valuable as a 10-yard completion on third-and-10.

Another area I wanted to incorporate in QBI was the combination of analytics and film. The best way to accurately account for what’s happening on the field is a marriage of the two — not one or the other — and that’s where PFF grades are helpful. There are things that happen in football that analytics can’t account for. While this might surprise you, I am happy to admit that.

The last thing to know before you examine the QBI standings from 2025 is my scale of measurement. I’ve taken a page from baseball’s analytics handbook and am using 100 as “average,” similar to baseball’s weighted runs created plus (wRC+) statistic. This means you can expect a QBI of 100 to be average, 101 to be starter-level, 124 to be Pro Bowl-caliber and 133 to be considered an All-Pro.

The Caleb conundrum

Why is Caleb Williams ranked all the way down there at No. 23? Let me explain QBI’s process.

First and foremost, the Chicago Bears quarterback finished 21st in dropback success rate among qualified quarterbacks last year. When a QB rates below-average at consistently manufacturing successful plays, that’s a tough place to start. Then we move on to the supporting cast: QBI really didn’t like how inefficient Williams was despite boasting pristine protection; my model graded the Bears’ offensive line as the top pass-protecting unit in the NFL in 2025.

QBI did like that Williams avoided negative plays, as he limited both interceptions and sacks, but overall, the down-to-down efficiency just wasn’t there. This doesn’t mean QBI won’t grade Williams much higher this year with improved play. In fact, you can make the argument that QBI thinks Williams still has a lot of room to grow, and that should excite Bears fans about how high his ceiling is. But for now, Williams has work to do before QBI considers him a top-10 quarterback.

Away we go. The NFL season is finally upon us, quenching the thirst we’ve had since the end of the Super Bowl. The draft, free agency, training camp — all critical events that set the table for this moment, as we find out who can win the biggest prize in football.

This year we’re delivering our Week 1 power rankings along with the tiers we think each team belongs in. From the dominant organizations seemingly destined for greatness to those who are already circling draft night in 2027 to find a way to get better.

Tier 1: Super Bowl Contenders

Nobody in our top five should really surprise anyone. These are the teams that are the elite of the elite, the cream of the crop, the organizations that either have everything together they need to hoist the Lombardi Trophy, or have issues so minor they won’t play a major role in their success. These are the teams that would stun us if they missed the playoffs, or got eliminated early.

The Rams speak for themselves in this tier. The big question comes at the back end with the Ravens, who perennially get ranked high because they should have all the tools to make it, but end up with a fatal flaw in the playoffs. This year we see new head coach Jesse Minter having the capability to get them over that hump.

No. 1: Los Angeles Rams

No. 2: Seattle Seahawks

No. 3: Buffalo Bills

No. 4: Philadelphia Eagles

No. 5: Baltimore Ravens

Tier 2: Super Bowl Potential

The second tier of teams houses organizations that are all extremely talented. “Super Bowl Potential” means precisely that: They have the table set to make a run to the big game, assuming a couple of key wrinkles get ironed out, or they see a breakout performance that puts them over the top.

Where this tier gets interesting is in the manner of issue they deal with. The Chiefs are hoping to finally have a run game, the Lions and Packers have struggled when they get to the playoffs, the Pats are still young and need to find themselves — while the 49ers, well, they just need to be healthy.

These teams would neither surprise us if they made it to the Super Bowl, or shock us if they lost early in the playoffs.

No. 6: Kansas City Chiefs

No. 7: Detroit Lions

No. 8: Green Bay Packers

No. 9: New England Patriots

No. 10: San Francisco 49ers

Tier 3: Super Bowl Dark Horses

Easily the most fun tier of NFL teams are the Dark Horses. These are organizations that have a lot of the traits you want to see from a contender, but each possesses a fatal flaw that is impossible to ignore as well. If we go back to 2025 and look at the Seahawks we knew their defense was going to be great, but the massive question was whether or not Sam Darnold could take the step to lead a contender — obviously that happen.

This is all to say that having a flaw on paper doesn’t mean you can’t win; it just means you need to shock the world. It’s possible that all these teams can do just that.

No. 11: Houston Texans

No. 12: Los Angeles Chargers

No. 13: Chicago Bears

No. 14: Cincinnati Bengals

No. 15: Denver Broncos

No. 16: Dallas Cowboys

Tier 4: Playoff Caliber

Hitting Tier 4 we have the teams that have the pieces to make the playoffs, and that’s more or less their ceiling. There’s a mixture of lacking top-end talent, one side of the ball which is highly problematic, or simply being too young to really believe they can put a run together.

The shared DNA in this tier is that these organizations are all on a knife’s edge. They could continue to build and become contenders, or have a few things falter and tumble back to rebuild mode. The margins are that narrow.

No. 17: Jacksonville Jaguars

No. 18: Pittsburgh Steelers

No. 19: Tampa Bay Buccaneers

No. 20: Carolina Panthers

No. 21: Indianapolis Colts

No. 22: Minnesota Vikings

Tier 5: Works in Progress

The teams in this tier are developing parts of their rosters, but there are pieces in place that we truly like. It would not surprise us to see some, or all, of these teams listed in the “Teams in the Hunt” category on the playoff graphics we start to see around the holiday season.

But there are questions with each team. Will the Commanders offensive line be as bad as reports out of training camp sound? Can Jaxson Dart take a step forward in Year Two? Can Cam Ward? And while the Atlanta Falcons have talent around the quarterback position, can the combination of Michael Penix Jr./Tua Tagovailoa/Cooper Rush/Jack Strand get them the ball?

And what is that old adage? If you have three quarterbacks, then you have none?

What does it mean when a team keeps four?

No. 23: Washington Commanders

No. 24: New Orleans Saints

No. 25: New York Giants

No. 26: Tennessee Titans

No. 27: Atlanta Falcons

Tier 6: The Tankathon Tier

Here we find the teams at the bottom of the league, at least to start the year.

We are affectionately calling this the “Tankathon Tier,” as these fanbases will likely wear out that website starting sometime in October.

This is not to say that these teams lack talent – there are certainly very good football players on each of these rosters. But for all of these teams, the questions outweigh the answers. And for many of these teams, the questions come at the most important position in the sport. All of them face questions at quarterback, and while the Raiders and Dolphins might believe the long-term answer at that position is already on the roster (Fernando Mendoza and Malik Willis), the jury is still out.

For the others, the website is www.tankathon.com. Bookmark it now. 

No. 28: Las Vegas Raiders

No. 29: Cleveland Browns

No. 30: Miami Dolphins

No. 31: New York Jets

No. 32: Arizona Cardinals

item.title: Bay State Ballers: How Massachusetts Ties Connect Miami’s Most Underrated X-Factors in Samson Okunlola and Omar Thornton
item.description: Brockton grit, Chestnut Hill polish - Okunlola and Thornton are Miami's quiet, Massachusetts-tested breakout stars.
item.content:encoded:
They won’t be confused for household names the way Malachi Toney or Darian Mensah are out of the gates. But tucked into the corners of Miami’s roster are two players whose paths both ran through the Commonwealth of Massachusetts – and both are quietly positioned to be two of the most important pieces of Miami’s championship puzzle in 2026.

Samson Okunlola grew up in Brockton, the self-proclaimed “City of Champions” and home to boxing legends Rocky Marciano and Marvelous Marvin Hagler. Omar Thornton never called Massachusetts home and actually hails from South Florida, but he spent two formative seasons in Chestnut Hill starring for Boston College before landing in Coral Gables. One built his game in the shadow of Titletown. The other built his in the shadow of the Heights. Both are about to be counted on to anchor entirely different phases as anchors of the offense and defense of Miami’s push for a national title – and both have real NFL money riding on how this season goes.

Forged in New England Winters

There’s an old, half-joking belief in football circles that toughness gets manufactured somewhere north of the Mason-Dixon line, and the two seasons Thornton spent grinding through Chestnut Hill practices in sideways sleet and the years Okunlola spent building his frame through actual Massachusetts winters aren’t nothing. Practicing through a Boston November – biting wind off the Chestnut Hill Reservoir, fields that go from soggy to frozen solid overnight, offseason conditioning that doesn’t pause just because it’s 28 degrees outside – has a way of stripping away softness that South Florida’s football culture, for all its speed and flash, simply doesn’t demand of its players in the same way. Okunlola didn’t just get bigger and faster growing up outside Boston; he got hardened. Thornton didn’t just get more athletic playing two years at BC; he got tempered. Both showed up in Coral Gables as players who’d already been tested by an environment that doesn’t hand out easy days, and it shows up in how they play the game now – physical, unbothered, allergic to backing down.

Samson Okunlola: From Titletown to Left Tackle

Okunlola’s Massachusetts roots run deep. Brockton has produced champions across generations – Marciano went 49-0 as heavyweight champion of the world, Hagler terrorized the middleweight division for a decade – and Okunlola grew up carrying that same “Titletown” DNA, even if his path to stardom wound through Thayer Academy in nearby Braintree rather than Brockton’s own gyms. He left the state as the first five-star recruit in Massachusetts recruiting history, a distinction that still gets brought up any time a Bay State prospect blows up on the recruiting trail, and especially as the Northeast becomes more popular for recruiting purposes.

Since arriving in Coral Gables, Okunlola’s college career has been a study in patience even though he witnessed his fellow class of 2023 five star Cane offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa turn into a first round pick as early as possible this past April. Okunlola redshirted as a true freshman in 2023 after a season-ending knee injury limited him to three games, then bounced between tackle spots as a role player in 2024. Last season, with Miami’s line desperately needing steady, reliable depth, he shifted inside to left guard and quietly turned in one of the best pass-protection seasons on the entire roster – a valuable piece of Miami’s playoff run, which allowed for pressure-free performances in marquee moments against the likes of Ohio State, Ole Miss, and Indiana.

Now Okunlola is making the flip nobody outside the building necessarily expected: from guard back out to left tackle, the exact position he was a five-star recruit at coming out of high school. With Mauigoa gone to the NFL and Jackson Cantwell looking to begin his career at guard, it’s Okunlola – not the more hyped true freshman – who has taken the left tackle reps all fall and looked sound in the opener. It’s a full-circle moment for a player nicknamed “Pancake Honcho” for his ability to flatten defenders in the run game, and it puts him squarely in position to boost his NFL Draft stock in a way playing guard never could. Left tackle is where the money is, and Okunlola is finally getting his shot to prove he belongs there at the highest level.

The early returns are exactly what Miami hoped for. In the season-opening 45-6 rout of Stanford, Okunlola anchored the left side that thrived in pass protection. Darian Mensah went 27-of-30 for 400 yards and five touchdowns behind that protection, and while there’s a long season of SEC- and ACC-caliber pass rushers still to come, night one at left tackle went about as smoothly as Miami could’ve scripted it.

Omar Thornton: Miami’s Next Keionte Scott, By Way of Chestnut Hill

Thornton’s Massachusetts tie looks different on paper – he’s a South Florida kid through and through, a Plantation American Heritage product who grew up down the road from where he plays now – but he spent two full seasons wearing maroon and gold in Chestnut Hill before the portal brought him home. Over two years at Boston College, Thornton put together a legitimately productive resume: 111 tackles, 11.5 tackles for loss, five forced fumbles, and All-ACC Honorable Mention honors in 2025 while playing nearly 1,700 combined snaps for an Eagles program that gave him every opportunity to develop as a full-time starter.

That production is exactly why the Keionte Scott comparisons write themselves. Like Scott a year ago, Thornton arrives in Coral Gables as a name outside the building barely knows, stepping into a nickel role that demands exactly the kind of downhill physicality he flashed at BC. He already has built-in chemistry with this roster, too – Thornton played high school ball alongside both Malachi Toney and Xavier Lucas at American Heritage, which shortens the runway on any locker room or on-field cohesion questions.

It also helps that Thornton didn’t develop in a vacuum at Boston College. For both of his seasons on The Heights, he lined up in the same secondary as KP Price, a Baltimore native who’s since become one of the most respected safeties in the ACC. Price led BC in tackles in both 2024 and 2025, earned All-ACC Second-Team honors as a team captain last season, and was tabbed to the 2026 Preseason All-ACC Team as one of the conference’s premier defensive backs. Getting two full years of practice reps and game-day tutelage alongside a player of Price’s caliber and leadership pedigree isn’t nothing – it’s exactly the kind of environment that accelerates a young defensive back’s development, and it shows in how quickly Thornton was able to step into a full-time starting role and produce immediately once the opportunity came.

There’s real refinement left in his game – Thornton’s missed-tackle rate at BC was high, and he gave up his fair share of plays in coverage – but the same could’ve been said about Scott’s tape before he arrived at Miami and turned into a household name with a pick-six against Ohio State in the Cotton Bowl. In fact, one game into the season, Cristobal is already noting Thornton “changes us with his physicality.” If Hetherman’s staff can sand down the rough edges the way they did with Scott, Thornton has every physical tool to be the next name Miami fans are chanting by December.

Two Unsung X-Factors, Two Draft Boards Watching

Neither Okunlola nor Thornton is walking into 2026 with the kind of hype that follows Cantwell, Mensah, or Toney. That’s precisely what makes them so dangerous. Okunlola is a former five-star finally getting his shot at his natural position on an offensive line that’s proven, two years running, capable of turning good tackle play into early round quarterback production. Thornton is a proven ACC playmaker stepping into a defense that already showed it knows exactly how to unlock a physical, ball-hawking defensive back from the transfer portal.

Both have NFL scouts watching closely. Okunlola’s tape at left tackle this fall will determine whether he’s playing his way into Day 2 conversations after years of position uncertainty. Thornton, with two years of eligibility remaining, has a chance to build the kind of standout season at Miami that turns “solid ACC safety” into “future NFL Draft pick” the same way it did for Scott.

Don’t be surprised if this time next year both names have crept a lot further up draft boards than anyone expects right now. After the 2026 debut at left tackle, Okunlola is already drawing early-round buzz from mock draft analysts for the 2027 class. With some evaluators pointing to his rare combination of length, power, and athletic testing as first-round-caliber traits if he strings together a clean season at left tackle – the exact kind of helmet-off-the-couch potential that made him the first five-star recruit in Massachusetts history in the first place. Thornton isn’t far behind. A full, healthy season as Miami’s every-down nickel, in a defense that’s already shown it knows how to turn productive-but-raw defensive backs into high picks, gives him a real runway to push into Day 2 territory of his own.

Second-or-third-round value feels possible for both. The ceiling, if this season goes the way Miami expects, is a lot higher than that.

Titletown and the Heights don’t have much in common on the surface. But this season, they’re both quietly fueling two of the most important breakout stories on Miami’s roster — one anchoring the blindside, the other patrolling the back end, both hardened by New England winters, and both with a chip on their shoulder and a draft profile to build.

item.title: How the Falcons can start reviving a dejected fanbase with low expectations
item.description: In what seems likely to be another season without playoff football in Atlanta, worthwhile progress is still possible.
item.content:encoded:
Whenever a team finds itself alone in a category except for the New York Jets, it most likely has fallen on hard times. That’s where the Falcons are when it comes to playoff appearances since 2020. After the Panthers won the NFC South last season, only the Falcons and Jets remain as teams that haven’t made the playoffs in the 2020s.

Considering the state of the NFC South since Tom Brady retired after the 2022 season, it’s unfathomable that the Falcons haven’t won the division. They made significant free agency investments in 2023 and 2024 to put themselves in a position to bring playoff football back to Atlanta. They swept the team that finished in first place in Tampa Bay in 2024. The front office went all in on drafting two highly regarded edge rushers in the first round to address the most significant flaw on the roster last year. None of it has resulted in making a playoff appearance.

Three consecutive disappointing years have led to multiple coaching changes, four starting quarterbacks, and exceptional players on both sides of the ball deserving so much better. It has left a fanbase largely jaded. From the Arthur Smith-Desmond Ridder debacle in 2023 to Kirk Cousins collapsing in 2024 to Raheem Morris losing control last year, the consistent failure has been heavy for a franchise that can’t figure things out.

Matt Ryan becoming the Falcons’ President of Football provided a much-needed spark. It will take much more than the return of a franchise legend to inject optimism into a franchise that hasn’t made the playoffs since Nick Foles’ peak. New coach Kevin Stefanski needs to build a true identity. Ian Cunningham must prove his promising start as general manager leads to lasting success. That starts with young players emerging on one of the league’s oldest rosters.

Whether the Falcons make the playoffs or not won’t determine their success in 2026. Several personnel concerns exist across the roster, none bigger than at the sport’s most important position. Putting playoff expectations on a team that doesn’t know which quarterback will start the most games for them isn’t practical. That shouldn’t prevent them from making strides as a franchise. The revamped coaching staff and promising talent are there for genuine growth in Atlanta.

Overcoming quarterback uncertainty through coaching

Other than Kevin O’Connell, it’s hard to find a current head coach who has endured more quarterback instability yet still found ways to succeed than Stefanski. You lose count trying to remember all the different signal callers he had to work with for six seasons in Cleveland. That’s a challenge the two-time Coach of the Year will have to take on again in 2026. The difference is he has a more solidified offensive infrastructure with legitimate firepower.

A trio of Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts creates exciting possibilities no matter who is under center. An offensive line returning four starters, with Bill Callahan coaching them, provides stability that was lost in his final years in Cleveland. The pieces are there to construct an efficient offense that can outscore teams, even with the glaring quarterback limitations.

Diversifying the run game will be crucial in controlling tempo and wearing down opposing fronts. After relying too heavily on outside zone for multiple seasons, adding more gap-scheme concepts should bring more consistency on the ground.

Increasing play-action usage and more varied formations are other potential schematic assets that Stefanski brings to the table. The overall offense needed a total reset after it became so predictable under Zac Robinson.

Questions linger about the game plan, whether it’s for Tua Tagovailoa early in the year and perhaps Michael Penix Jr. later on. There’s also skepticism about Tommy Rees as offensive coordinator, as Cleveland ranked 30th in EPA per play when he took over play-calling duties in Week 10 last season.

While the Falcons’ offense is significantly more talented, can Rees work with Stefanski to help maximize the quarterback’s capabilities? Whether it’s a quick-pass, heavy RPO system with Tagovailoa or a more aggressive shotgun-based plan with Penix Jr., the Falcons invested too much into their offense to be below average.

Stefanski worked wonders with Cleveland in 2020 and 2023 when expectations weren’t exactly high. Some of it came from utilizing heavier personnel packages, running 12 and 13 looks,  creating more high-percentage looks in the passing game, and putting the offense in better down-and-distances. Attacking defenses with a wide variety of screens was another key component to his success.

These are ideal strategies the Falcons can use, given where they stand at quarterback and wide receiver. That said, Stefanski must be decisive, alongside Rees, to execute his vision with the right quarterback on the current roster. Based on how much Tagovailoa has struggled this summer, Penix Jr. appears to be his best option, but Penix is not ready to start just yet.

Staying afloat defensively while a stellar secondary establishes itself

Jeff Ulbrich deserves enormous praise for the defense’s elevation last season. After his return to Atlanta initially underwhelmed many people, he silenced critics with his pressure plans and coverage variation. The franchise record for most sacks in a season was broken without a game-changing edge rusher on the roster, with defensive line coach Nate Ollie also deserving major credit. While James Pearce Jr. broke the franchise record for most sacks by a rookie in a season, he didn’t take over games. It took a cohesive effort for them to overwhelm some of the league’s best offenses in dramatic upset victories.

Many of the players who were at the forefront of their success aren’t with the team going into the season. According to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s Daniel Flick, only 28.1% of the sack production will be on the opening-day roster. That total will increase when Pearce Jr. returns from suspension in Week 9. That won’t change the fact that this is a major obstacle for Ulbrich to overcome.

Losing Jalon Walker for the season was a devastating blow after his promising rookie season. While it’s encouraging that the new regime was proactive in signing ZaDarius Smith and trading for Gervon Dexter Sr. to add talent up front, it’s difficult to envision the front imposing their will on many offensive lines.

That not only increases the pressure on Ulbrich to call more twists and blitzes. It raises expectations for an ultra-talented secondary to lead the overall unit.

Expectations must be high when a group features an All-Pro safety, Pro Bowl-caliber cornerback, an emerging ball-hawking safety, and two promising cornerbacks, as well as a well-regarded secondary coach in Justin Hood. It likely won’t happen on opening day, but Jessie Bates, A.J. Terrell, Xavier Watts, Avieon Terrell, and Billy Bowman Jr. should be on the field together at some point. Assembling those five players should fluster quarterbacks and produce turnovers. 

I wrote about how special the secondary can be a month ago. While Mike Hughes will start the season, things could change as Avieon Terrell proves he can handle playing significant snaps and Bowman Jr. is healthy. Bates and Watts are consistently around the ball, attempting to make game-changing plays. A.J. Terrell is quietly coming off one of his better years. This group has all the pieces to take a significant leap to become one of the league’s best.

Along with Divine Deablo, it’s the best hope to keep the defense stabilized after enduring significant losses. Brandon Dorlus’ rapid ascendance, with Maason Smith and Dexter Sr. becoming dependable, will be pivotal. The possibility of Kendal Daniels or Harold Perkins Jr. emerging as a three-down linebacker creates more long-term progression for a unit that will feel the loss of Kaden Elliss in a multitude of ways. 

There are no certainties up front, but the unit is talented enough to stay solidified, managing through concerns at edge rusher, interior tackle, and inside linebacker opposite Deablo. Ulbrich has proven his units can thrive while coping with personnel flaws in certain areas. He knows how to maximize limited and unproven players’ skill sets while bringing out the best in his leaders.

His defense still has franchise cornerstone players in Bates, Deablo, and Terrell, with young standouts like Watts and Dorlus taking on expanded roles. How the unit holds up and develops in the trenches will determine whether they stay on a steady path or revert to the dreaded space of attempting to bend, not break.

Don’t beat yourself. Rise to the occasion against the upper echelon

One of the main reasons the Falcons couldn’t win a historically bad NFC South last season or a very winnable division in 2024 was the previous coaching staff’s propensity to mismanage games in crucial moments. In what was essentially a playoff-eliminating defeat to Washington,

Morris failed to use one of his two remaining timeouts on a potential game-winning drive with Penix Jr. making his second career start. In a primetime loss to San Francisco, the defense had only ten players on the field on 3rd and 13 with less than three minutes left, leading to a 17-yard completion to Christian McCaffrey.

To quote my colleague Kevin Knight from his piece last December about Morris, the Falcons played losing football under him. The new regime can’t afford to make similar self-inflicted errors to put players at a disadvantage.

It happened far too often under the previous regime, from constant pre-snap penalties to special teams breakdowns. Players must be held accountable in instances, but those issues becoming a weekly habit indicates how poorly coached the team was.

The Falcons will lose their share of games in 2026. They face five playoff teams in their first seven games, which is followed by matchups against the Bengals, Chiefs, and Vikings. Let’s not forget the daunting task of facing the Ravens at the start of the season. They will be overmatched at times. They will take their dosages of punishment on both sides of the ball. What they can’t do is crumble because of their lack of discipline. 

Stefanski needs to have this group ready to compete in these arduous battles. They proved they can defy expectations last season by beating the Bills and Rams on Monday Night Football. They should have beaten the Colts when they were on top of the AFC. The same can be said for when they nearly beat the Patriots. There hasn’t been a significant drop-off in talent where they can’t be competitive against the Steelers, Packers, Bears, and 49ers.

Moral victories don’t exist in locker rooms, but frequent one-sided blowout losses can eradicate the belief within an organization. Playing inspired, competitive football with the knack of earning divisional wins and pushing potential Super Bowl contenders to the brink is the realistic recipe for success in 2026.

All-Pro caliber players continue to drive the team. Young difference-makers start to emerge on both sides of the ball. The coaching staff establishes an identity that serves as a launching pad for future success. Times will get very difficult for the Falcons this season.

That doesn’t make it a foregone conclusion that this year will be a total calamity as games become irrelevant come December. They have the foundational pieces to overcome tough defeats and push forward into 2027.

item.title: Can the Commanders upset the Eagles in Philly to open the season and seize control of the NFC East?
item.description: David Blough and Sean Mannion look to elevate Jayden Daniels and Jalen Hurts; Daronte Jones steps out of Flores' shadow
item.content:encoded:
Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer, Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026.

From John Portis:

Things have changed a lot since June, when Bill-in-Bangkok wrote his preview of this week’s season opener against the defending NFC East champs in Philly.

The loss of Laremy Tunsil turned up the heat on the Commanders’ 2026 season before it even started, while the absence of Nick Allegretti for most of training camp put the spotlight on Adam Peters’ decision, back in February, to move on from center Tyler Biadasz.

A move to injured reserve with a designation to return for Trey Amos has shaken confidence in a secondary that struggled last season, but the addition of Stefon Diggs has been huge for the outlook of the Commanders’ offense. Sports writers have soured on the Commanders early, even as the coaches and players have reaffirmed their confidence in one another.

The Washington Commanders have two new coordinators in David Blough and Daronte Jones. Blough hasn’t unveiled his new offense, but we know to expect the quarterback under center more, plenty of motion, and play-action. Penalties have been a concern discussed by head coach Dan Quinn throughout training camp. Daronte Jones has kept his defense under wraps, but occasional glimpses — like a six-man blitz versus Detroit — show a blitz-heavy scheme with disguised pressures and coverages.

New Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion is also installing an under center, motion-heavy offense, with a core philosophy of providing clarity for Jalen Hurts before the snap. That offense should be timing- and rhythm-based.

Eagles defensive coordinator, Vic Fangio, returns to run his two-high safety system designed to disguise coverages pre-snap behind disciplined front seven execution. There seems to be some thought among Eagles fans that, as a rookie defensive coordinator, Daronte Jones is a nice slow pitch start for Mannion, but Jones already appears to be one of the more competent coaches on Dan Quinn’s staff.

The new offensive schemes in Philly and Washington represent significant shifts for the quarterbacks of both teams. Simply huddling the offense on a regular basis will be new for Jayden Daniels. Last season, the average NFL offense huddled about 82 percent of the time. With Daniels on the field, the Commanders huddled just about 32 percent of the time. So far, Jayden Daniels has looked sharp during training camp and practice with the word “surgical” being used a lot, but after taking an ugly three offensive snaps in the 2nd preseason game, Dan Quinn shut Jayden and the rest of the 1st-team offense down for the rest of that game and the final one in Baltimore. There is a lot to project, but with new offensive weapons, Daniels should be effective if the line can give him time to work.

Jalen Hurts, on the other hand, has reportedly had a rocky transition so far, throwing numerous interceptions in training camp. Mannion’s offense tasks him with throwing in rhythm as a wide receiver comes out of his breaks, which does not appear to be a completely natural fit for Hurts. Mannion is expected to want to work the middle of the field where Jalen has little experience. If the Commanders can disrupt the timing of the Eagles’ passing attack, there should be an opportunity for the secondary to corral some interceptions.

The Commanders have invested heavily in edge talent, adding both Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson in the offseason. If both are healthy, they will lead the pass rushing attack for the Washington. Jones will be counting on the two edges to speed up Hurts’ clock and protect Washington’s secondary. The Eagles return Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis; the pair working against new Commanders starting center Nick Allegretti will be a matchup to watch.

Not listed in Hog Haven’s summer preview, which was published in June (and which you can read below), is Philly’s trade acquisition of Dontayvion Wicks. First-round selection Makai Lemon suffered a hamstring injury during OTAs and experienced some setbacks, so it should be Wicks and Smith to start following the trade of A.J. Brown. Washington also added wide receiver Stefon Diggs, who will look to breakout in Washington’s remade offense versus Eagles free agent addition Riq Woolen. Both offensive coordinators prioritize three-down ability in their running backs, so we should see plenty of Saquon Barkley and Commanders’ free agent addition Rachaad White in the receiving game.

This is a tough matchup for the Commanders to start their season, with the difficulty level ratcheted up on the road. The team’s best hope is the Eagles’ offense takes longer to gel than Washington’s defense. If the defense can contain the game early and allow Jayden Daniels time to settle in, he could provide enough game-changing plays to give his team the chance to walk away with an upset win in a divisional season opener on the road.
