Week 1 Preview: Washington Commanders at Philadelphia Eagles

Date: September 13, 2026, 4:25 p.m. ET
Location: Lincoln Financial Field, Philadelphia, PA

(The two teams play again at Northwest Stadium in Landover in Week 8)

When the 2026 NFL season kicks off, this Week 1 divisional game in Philadelphia will provide a major test for two teams entering the year with completely different mindsets. For Washington, it is about bouncing back from a rough 2025 where poor defensive play and offensive regression forced them into another early draft pick. Philadelphia, on the other hand, had a highly successful regular season where they won the NFC East and locked up a playoff spot. While their 2025 season ended with a frustrating first-round exit in the postseason, the Eagles enter the ’26 season as the defending NFC East champs, looking to defend that title and actually win a playoff game this time around.

While Washington spent the offseason making massive roster moves to help third-year quarterback Jayden Daniels, the Eagles are in a fighting retreat against years of over-leveraging the salary cap, losing key players in free agency but working hard to replenish the roster through the draft as they struggle to remain at the top of the NFC East.

The Commanders bolstered their offense by adding dynamic skill players like running backs Rachaad White & Kaytron Allen, wide receiver Antonio Williams, and tight end Chig Okonkwo. They also completely overhauled their defensive unit, aggressively using free agency to add players at every level and drafting linebacker Sonny Styles with the 7th overall pick to anchor a scheme run by new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. Meanwhile, the Eagles are entering another transition period of their own under Nick Sirianni, breaking in a brand new offensive scheme after parting ways with their previous offensive coordinator.

The coaching matchup and scheme alignment

This game features a battle between two coaching staffs under pressure to get better results than they did in 2025.

In Washington, Dan Quinn shook things up by letting go of defensive coordinator Joe Whitt and offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury. Under new DC Daronte Jones, the Commanders are switching to a highly aggressive, versatile defensive system that should look similar to the blitz-heavy, multi-front concepts Jones learned from Brian Flores when he was with the Minnesota Vikings. Washington’s defense will most likely change between 3-4 and 4-3 looks while using a lot of pre- and post-snap disguises to confuse the quarterback. In the secondary, Jones’ system relies on keeping plays in front of them with safe zone coverages, allowing their defenders to break downhill and make physical tackles and make plays on the ball.

View Link

Under new offensive coordinator David Blough, the Commanders are moving away from Kliff Kingsbury’s spread-heavy concepts to implement a more traditional, West Coast-inspired passing attack. Blough’s system is expected to focus on quick-game rhythm, strict timing, and pre-snap motion to create mismatches across the middle of the field. While this scheme will require Jayden Daniels to play more from the pocket and get the ball out fast, his elite athleticism should provide a critical safety valve when the play structure breaks down.

Philadelphia counters with head coach Nick Sirianni, who has once again overhauled his offensive staff. The Eagles hired Sean Mannion as their new offensive coordinator, marking the fifth consecutive year the team has had a new play-caller. Even more challenging, the Eagles will be playing their first season since 2012 without legendary offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, who left the team in February.

Mannion’s system is expected to lean on a modified West Coast approach that values quick decisions, but the biggest hurdle will be how fast the offensive line adapts to new OL coach Chris Kuper. On defense, veteran coordinator Vic Fangio returns to run his classic light-box, split-safety zone schemes, which are designed to prevent big passing plays. With his protege Christian Parker taking over as DC in Dallas, the Commanders should have the added advantage of playing 4 games per year (Eagles & Cowboys home & away) against a Fangio-style defense.

Quarterback showdown

One of the central storylines of this opening game is the matchup between two highly athletic NFC East quarterbacks looking to silence their critics. For Washington, Jayden Daniels proved he could be a highly efficient leader during his rookie year but spent much of 2025 battling through injuries and some on-field setbacks. Under new offensive coordinator David Blough, the Commanders are completely abandoning Kliff Kingsbury’s old spread concepts. Blough is implementing a traditional under-center, timing-based passing attack that uses pre-snap motion to create easy throws across the middle and play-action opportunities. While this requires Daniels to stay in the pocket more and make quick decisions, his elite scrambling ability will still be the ultimate backup plan when a play breaks down.

The Eagles answer with Jalen Hurts, who is looking to bounce back after an inconsistent 2025 campaign. Hurts still possesses dual-threat capabilities that challenge defenses, but he will have to adjust to Sean Mannion’s new rhythm passing game. As is the case with Washington and Jayden Daniels, the Eagles will look to put Hurts under center more often, using hard play-action and designed quarterback runs to keep Washington’s aggressive front seven off balance. How well Hurts commands this new offense without his longtime offensive line coach will be a massive factor in Week 1.

The roster: Free agency, trades & the draft

On the player personnel side, Howie Roseman continued to be aggressive across free agency, trades, and the draft in an effort to counter the bleeding of talented veteran players from the roster:

Free Agency & Trades:

The Philadelphia Eagles took some needed steps to re-stock their roster for the 2026 season through free agent acquisitions, key re-signings, and 8 draft picks. They also swapped a player for future draft capital in a major June 1st trade.

Trades

Perhaps the most notable roster move this offseason was trading WR AJ Brown to the New England Patriots for a 2028 1st-round pick and a 2027 5th-rounder.

Also, the Eagles executed trades during the NFL Draft, sending two third-round picks (a 2026 compensatory pick and a 2027 third-round pick) to the Vikings for edge rusher Jonathan Greenard and a late-round pick. Shortly after the trade was finalized, the Eagles signed Greenard to a four-year, $100 million contract extension.

Other Key veteran moves and signings included:

  • Riq Woolen (CB)
  • Grant Calcaterra (TE)
  • Dallas Goedert (TE): Re-signed
  • Jonathan Jones (DB)

Key losses:

  • S Reed Blankenship
  • LB Nakobe Dean
  • WR Jahan Dotson
  • Edge Brandon Graham
  • CB Adoree’ Jackson
  • Edge Jaelan Phillips

The 2026 NFL Draft

Round 1, No. 20 overall: Makai Lemon, WR, USC – The Eagles traded up to select the 2025 Biletnikoff Award winner. He is expected to start immediately as a top slot target with A.J. Brown’s departure.


Round 2, No. 54: Eli Stowers, TE, Vanderbilt – Philadelphia drafted the 2025 John Mackey Award winner to serve as their long-term answer at tight end, given that Dallas Goedert is 31 and on a one-year deal.
Round 3, No. 68: Markel Bell, OT, Miami – A massive developmental tackle prospect standing at 6-foot-9 and 346 pounds. He possesses rare length (an 87.13-inch wingspan) and will provide depth behind veterans Lane Johnson and Landon Dickerson.
Round 5, No. 178: Cole Payton, QB, North Dakota State – A dual-threat, left-handed quarterback; Payton joins a room featuring Jalen Hurts, Andy Dalton, and Tanner McKee while the team transitions to Sean Mannion’s new offense.
Round 6, No. 207: Micah Morris, G, Georgia – Added to provide immediate interior depth behind Tyler Steen and Landon Dickerson. He allowed only one sack during his college career while playing both guard spots.
Round 7, No. 244: Cole Wisniewski, S, Texas Tech – A physical safety brought in to compete for a roster spot and fill out a thin safety room following the free-agency departure of Reed Blankenship.
Round 7, No. 251: Uar Bernard, DT, International Player Pathway – A raw, highly athletic Nigerian prospect who has never played football. At 306 pounds, he ran a 40-yard dash in the 4.6 range and represents a long-term developmental project.
Round 7, No. 252: Keyshawn James-Newby, Edge, New Mexico – The final pick of Philly’s draft class, KJN led his college team with nine sacks in 2025 and will fight to earn a rotational pass-rushing role this summer.

Historical context and storylines

The Commanders and Eagles share one of the oldest and most bitter rivalries in the NFL — one in which the Commanders hold the lead in overall W-L record at 91-87-5. While Philadelphia has largely controlled the NFC East over the last few years, Washington has consistently played them incredibly tough. In fact, even during down years, the Commanders have managed to pull off surprising upsets against the Eagles. A win in this 2026 Week 1 game would see the series stand at 3-3 in the Dan Quinn era, while a Washington loss would tilt the table to 2-4 in favor of the Eagles since the start of the ’24 season when Quinn took over as head coach.

The main storyline surrounding this game is the massive amount of schematic change on both sidelines. Opening the season against a fierce divisional opponent while breaking in two new offensive coordinators and one defensive coordinator means that the team that makes fewer mental mistakes will have a massive advantage. Additionally, playing at Lincoln Financial Field is always a hostile environment for road teams, giving the Eagles a distinct home-field emotional edge. Philly is favored in early betting lines, so the Commanders will face a tough road test against a good team and a tough crowd as Washington looks to reverse fortune in 2026.

item.title: NFL power rankings Week 1: Did a Super Bowl 60 team miss top five?
item.description: As the 2026 NFL season kicks off, last year's two best teams already find themselves looking up at this year's apparent challengers.
item.content:encoded:
NFL power rankings entering Week 1 of the 2026 season (previous rank in parentheses):

1. Los Angeles Rams (1): Can you name their No. 3 wideout? Perhaps the only apparent Achilles of this star-studded lineup is the seeming lack of quality and experience that resides directly behind the big names on the depth chart.

2. Seattle Seahawks (2): We know the reigning champs can play suffocating defense. But Wednesday night will provide early insight to the trajectory of an offense now run by rookie coordinator Brian Fleury and featuring first-round RB Jadarian Price and WR Rashid Shaheed, a mid-season acquisition in 2025. It could be a far more explosive unit.

3. Denver Broncos (3): Is a team that was arguably − inarguably? − the AFC's best in 2025 getting enough Super Bowl love in 2026? Almost certainly not, though that might have something to do with Denver's brutal first-half schedule, which includes the entire NFC West and two other division winners from last season.

4. Buffalo Bills (4): The feel-good vibes in Western New York are hard to ignore, even amid all the changes for what's become a perennial AFC power … and, perhaps for the first time in more than three decades, the AFC's preeminent force.

5. Chicago Bears (5): "I want to have the highest-scoring offense ever, which happens to be the 2013 Denver Broncos," HC Ben Johnson told The Athletic last month. That Peyton Manning-led Denver squad scored 37.9 points per game, roughly 50% more than the 2025 Bears, before it managed eight in a humiliating Super Bowl 48 loss. Eye on the ball coach, maybe not the record book?

6. New England Patriots (11): If not for the distraction invited by 2025 Coach of the Year Mike Vrabel, you'd have to say the Pats had a very productive offseason − culminating with CB Christian Gonzalez's now-completed extension.

7. San Francisco 49ers (7): Are there electrical substations in Melbourne? The Niners seem likely to have nearly all of their injured stars − and plenty of in-country rest − as they prepare to kick off the season in Australia. But will it all be enough against the mighty Rams, who have won four of five against San Francisco?

8. Cincinnati Bengals (8): A defense that quietly stabilized after Thanksgiving last year might now be good enough to actually win this team a few games while permitting QB Joe Burrow to routinely operate underneath center.

9. Dallas Cowboys (9): Taken the Super Bowl Kool-Aid here? Not mad at you. But LG Tyler Smith's thumb surgery is the latest question about an offensive line that coach Brian Schottenheimer needs − and expects − dominance from if this club is to finally fulfill its always-outsized expectations.

10. Houston Texans (6): A defense that ceded more than 300 yards just six times last year might need to be even better until QB C.J. Stroud and an offense already coping with significant injuries can find its footing. But that could be a tall order given some of the high-powered attacks the Texans will face in the next two months.

11. Detroit Lions (10): If you subscribe to the theory that good teams are strong up the middle … then this one could be in trouble with C Cade Mays and starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph all at least a month away from playing. At least the Lions can lean on RB Jahmyr Gibbs, though there's zero safety net behind a bona fide star who's played fewer than 60% of this offense's snaps through the first three seasons of his career.

12. Baltimore Ravens (13): Pro Bowl DL Nnamdi Madubuike isn't quite Aaron Donald − who is? − yet his pending return to active duty might be the most crucial personnel development of Baltimore's offseason.

13. Kansas City Chiefs (12): While focus is justifiably trained on the Super Bowl MVP backfield of QB Patrick Mahomes and RB Kenneth Walker III, plenty should be devoted to a revamped defense − the secondary especially − that was quietly one of the league's stingiest in K.C.'s lost 2025 campaign.

14. Jacksonville Jaguars (15): While the Jags didn't draft Travis Hunter second overall last year thinking he'd be their WR4, if he's able to function as their top corner, the investment into him will be worth it.

15. Los Angeles Chargers (16): A team that lost its top offensive tackles early in the 2025 season begins 2026 with an entirely new trio of starters between OTs Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater − one further altered by the season-ending injury to free agent addition Tyler Biadasz.

16. Green Bay Packers (14): Their two best players in 2025? Almost inarguably OLB Micah Parsons and RB Josh Jacobs. When will either of them be on the field in 2026? Anyone's guess − but October could be lethal to the Pack if the duo remains absent.

17. Philadelphia Eagles (19): We know WR A.J. Brown is gone. What a new-look, Jalen Hurts-led offense − one that's largely been under wraps publicly all summer − will look like on game day is one of the league's more compelling mysteries entering the season.

18. Minnesota Vikings (17): Few teams ran the ball more efficiently last season (4.5 yards per attempt), yet few were less committed to the ground (24.1 rushes per game) than the Vikes. So what does new QB1 Kyler Murray mean on that front given his multi-dimensional abilities, yet proclivity to get injured?

19. New Orleans Saints (20): The engine of this playoff dark horse? How about an offensive line with three home-grown first-rounders and an expensive free-agent acquisition (G David Edwards) … unless it's a defense that surrendered just 262 yards per game over its final eight outings last season.

20. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (22): A legitimate postseason contender, albeit in a weak division? Or a maxed-out team held together by baling wire that will further disintegrate in 2027?

21. Pittsburgh Steelers (21): Another squad facing so many questions in 2027, particularly on the offensive side, probably should think long and hard before dumping more money into this defense (read: CB Joey Porter Jr.).

22. Indianapolis Colts (29): Seemingly healthy at long last, a team that's poured so much of its resources into QB Daniel Jones, WR Alec Pierce and CB Sauce Gardner is compelled to prove it's closer to the version that began 2025 with an 8-2 record … not the one which lost its final seven games.

23. New York Giants (23): Amid injuries and ongoing turnover at the position, including the recent release of Darius Slayton, rookie WR Malachi Fields quietly projects as one of Big Blue's most important players entering the opener.

24. Carolina Panthers (24): Looking for a major regression candidate? How about a division champion that finished in a three-way tie with an 8-9 record last year with six of those victories coming by exactly three points.

25. Washington Commanders (18): First-time NFL coordinators on both sides of the ball, wholesale personnel changes on defense and major questions on the offensive line after LT Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps last month? Does any team enter Week 1 with more uncertainty than this one?

26. Atlanta Falcons (25): How best to sum up the state of affairs here − aside from the QB uncertainty? None of the Falcons' past three first-round picks (QB Michael Penix Jr. and OLBs James Pearce Jr. and Jalon Walker) will be on the field for the foreseeable future.

27. New York Jets (30): They appear to have a nice nucleus of young players awaiting a QB to lead it for the long term − which is sure to give Week 1 opponent Robert Saleh flashbacks as he prepares the Titans to face his former team.

28. Tennessee Titans (26): They're counting on a young offense led by second-year QB Cam Ward to take a major step. They're counting on a defense infused with expensive free agent upgrades to take a major step. And they're counting heavily on Saleh to make it all work. Yet the preseason suggested they shouldn't necessarily count on instant results in 2026.

29. Las Vegas Raiders (28): Rookie Fernando Mendoza will become the first quarterback drafted No. 1 overall to start a season on the bench since Baker Mayfield in 2018. Maybe the Silver and Black would think differently if Mendoza had the benefit of facing Vegas' defense …

30. Cleveland Browns (27): Maybe the best way to get into position for a premium quarterback in the 2027 draft is to trade DE Myles Garrett … and start QB Deshaun Watson behind an offensive line that only retained one (spot) starter from 2026. Genius.

31. Arizona Cardinals (31): They could be a fun team to watch. Bummer their rookies got so beaten up in preseason and may need time to collectively get meaningful snaps, even amid a youth movement.

32. Miami Dolphins (32): How bad is a team with nearly $182 million in dead money on its salary cap? The Fins claimed seven players after the roster cutdown, which is highly indicative of how they feel about their talent quotient.

item.content:encoded:
Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis has not had the career he envisioned when he was selected in the third round of the 2022 NFL Draft. After two seasons in which he attempted a combined 66 passes in 11 games played for the Tennessee Titans, Willis was traded to the Green Bay Packers ahead of the 2024 season. He appeared in 11 games with 89 passes attempted in two years with the Packers before becoming a free agent this past offseason. The Dolphins jumped at the opportunity to sign Willis, provide him stability, and give him a chance to prove he is a capable starter in the league.

Now named the Dolphins’ starter, Willis has battled to earn this opportunity. The Palm Beach Post’s Joe Schad took a look at the perseverance and belief that it took for Willis to get to this point in a one-on-one interview:

Joe Schad: I think people appreciate perseverance. Some people feel like they were handed things and you have not been handed things. You have had to earn this. What qualities do you admire most in other people?

Malik Willis: Probably that perseverance that you talk about. I think that’s an important quality as far as life goes because you just never know what happens. All the ups and downs of life, if you can, you can always work towards something better. Regardless if it goes better or not, you can work towards something better. And that’s the opportunity. It keeps you going.

item.title: Rams used player 'guinea pigs' to help craft their Australia travel plan
item.description: The Rams' decision to leave as late as possible for their Australian season opener against the 49ers is based in part on player experiences from last year.
item.content:encoded:
Rams offensive lineman Kevin Dotson made the trip last spring. So did running back Kyren Williams, receiver Xavier Smith and defensive lineman Tyler Davis.

The four players traveled from Los Angeles to Australia as goodwill ambassadors.

But also as test cases.

First Dotson and Williams, and later Smith and Davis, endured the 16-hour flight from Los Angeles to Melbourne and the 14-hour flight home.

The players’ physical and mental experiences in flight, on the ground after arrival and during their stay, and after they returned was anecdotal data the Rams used when planning their trip for their season opener against the San Francisco 49ers at Melbourne Cricket Ground.

“They kind of used us as guinea pigs,” Dotson said, laughing, during training camp.

On Tuesday night, the Rams will board a plane bound for Melbourne, landing in Australia Thursday morning. After a night’s sleep, they will play the 49ers at 10:35 a.m. local time. (5:35 p.m. PDT).

The 49ers arrived in Australia last week.

Though the approaches are different, the Rams are no strangers to short turnarounds for games abroad.

Last season, after playing the Baltimore Ravens in Baltimore, the Rams stayed on the East Coast. The day before the game, they traveled to London. Players slept at a hotel, got up the next day and routed the Jacksonville Jaguars, 35-7.

“I think we saw that it worked,” Smith said, “and it’s like mimicking the same blueprint all over again.”

Coach Sean McVay has said that the decision to travel late to Australia was made after consultation with Reggie Scott, the Rams’ senior vice president of sports medicine and performance. And that all decisions are made with the best interests of players in mind.

“There are different approaches and theories,” McVay said, “but I do have a lot of trust in our group and we’ll see. Hopefully it works out.”

Weeks before McVay discussed specific travel plans and timetables, the players said they would trust the process, and that they did not anticipate an adverse effect on their performance.

“We’ll be fine,” Dotson said. “It’s going to be exhausting regardless, but the amount of rest we’ll get in between will be fine.”

Read more:Inside the 'almost unfair' Rams roster that makes it a Super Bowl title favorite

Like the Rams will do Tuesday, the four players departed on late-night flights. All said they watched several movies before falling asleep in long-haul, lie-flat seats.

“You feel like you’re at home going to sleep,” Davis said.

Said Smith: “I had slept eight to 10 hours, so once we landed, I was able to rock and roll.”

After arriving in the morning, the players stayed awake until evening.

“I really felt like if I went back to sleep it would mess me up,” Williams said.

For the last few weeks, the Rams have practiced in the late afternoon, which aligns body clock-wise with their impending morning kickoff in Melbourne.

Williams is confident in the Rams’ plan.

“It’s a business trip, and we gotta do what we gotta do,” Williams said. “So they’re going to find the best way to get us there in the best feeling, so all we got to do is trust them and go play.”

The Detroit Lions will open their 2026 regular season against the New Orleans Saints, hoping to rebound from a disappointing 2025 season. The Lions will get the advantage of hosting this game in Detroit, and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -6.5 points.

The Saints finished 2025 with a 6-11 record under first-time head coach (and former Lions backup quarterback) Kellen Moore. While they certainly underwhelmed, they finished the season strong, with four of those wins coming in the final five games of the regular season.

“This is a hungry opponent,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Monday. “It’s a lot of young, hungry players, talented players. You could see their progression as the season went on last year; they started playing pretty good football—minus Atlanta, in that last game.”

This offseason, the Saints prioritized upgrading their offense and plugging holes on defense.

One of the Saints’ biggest offseason moves was upgrading their guard positions. They signed starting left guard David Edwards in free agency, then added rookie Jeremiah Wright (a fourth-round pick) to the mix to challenge Cesar Ruiz, who is entering his seventh year as a starter (mainly at right guard) for the Saints.

They invested in youth at their skill positions, signing running back Travis Etienne to complement Alvin Kamara, but Kamara is dealing with an MCL injury and is expected to miss the opener. The Saints also drafted three wide receivers—Jordyn Tyson (first round), Bryce Lance (fourth), and Barion Brown (sixth)—and a tight end—Oscar Delp (third)—and all four are expected to contribute as rookies. Unfortunately, the Saints will have to wait to see the eighth overall pick take the field as Tyson landed on injured reserve with a hamstring injury and will miss the first four games of the season; Lance is expected to start in his place. Delp will open the season as TE3 and will challenge free-agent acquisition Noah Fant for TE2 reps.

On defense, the Saints lost one of their best players in starting linebacker Demario Davis, but re-signed Kaden Ellis to fill his role. Along the defensive line, 2023 first-round pick Bryan Bresee is out for the season with a torn ACL and is expected to be replaced by 2025 third-round pick Vernon Broughton. The Saints are banking on 2025 picks corner Quincy Riley (second) and nickelback Jonas Sanker (third) to step into vacated roles in their secondary.

The Lions and Saints will square off on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET at Ford Field in Detroit.

item.title: Instant grades for Christian Gonzalez contract extension with Patriots
item.description: The Patriots are keeping their top cornerback on a new four-year extension.
item.content:encoded:
On Labor Day, the New England Patriots and Christian Gonzalez birthed a contract extension to make him the highest-paid cornerback in the NFL. According to reports, the months-long process culminated on Monday in an agreement that will pay the 24-year-old $135 million over four years.

We don’t know the full structure of the deal yet, but the fact that it got signed in the first place is telling. So, let’s put a grade it.

Instant grades: Patriots sign CB Christian Gonzalez to 4-year, $135M extension

Bernd Buchmasser: The signs always pointed toward Gonzalez and the Patriots ultimately reaching an agreement, but the timeline and eventual scope of the deal was where the uncertainty lied. It took a while for those questions to get resolved, but doing so before the start of the season is the best-case scenario even though it meant a massive investment on the team’s part. | Grade: A+

Andrew Guindon: This is a regime that’s emphasized retaining and rewarding its top talent, and that’s what the Patriots ultimately did with Gonzalez. Having a true premier shutdown cornerback on your roster, such as Gonzalez is a luxury in the NFL. Those are the types of players you pay while Drake Maye is still under his rookie contract. He showcased how impactful he can be in the biggest moments during last season’s Super Bowl, and now he’s under contract through 2031. | Grade: A+

Pat Lane: I don’t care how long it took, they locked up their CB1 and sent a message that they are going to reward guys for their play and commitment to the team. I don’t love the fact that Robert Kraft spoke about it to the media, because he opened the door on that, but the fact that they signed him, and had it just above Devon Witherspoon is fantastic. | Grade: A+

Matt St. Jean: There were some questions about how Christian Gonzalez might fit with Mike Vrabel’s scheme, but those were erased down to stretch as he embraced physicality and then showcased his premier coverage skills in the Super Bowl. Gonzalez is the kind of player who can take any opposing receiver out of the game and erase any chance for big plays in his area of the field. That’s highly valuable, and worth the price the Patriots paid. | Grade: A+

Dylan Klayman: Gonzalez as a top corner in the league deserved to be paid like it, especially after his standout performance throughout the playoffs. Locking him up before the season starts is huge, so it doesn’t create another distraction, and your CB1 can just go out there and play. Obviously, it would have been nice if there wasn’t a whole story in the media from Kraft about the contract, and Gonzalez’s camp getting mad about it. But at least it is in the rear view mirror now, and you have one of your best players signed for the foreseeable future. | Grade: A+

item.title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 5 Days Remaining
item.description: We continue our countdown to the Panthers opening the 2026 season against the Chicago Bears
item.content:encoded:
Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial.

#5. Steve Smith, Sr

Throughout the history of sports, there have been many players who play with a chip on their shoulder. This skill of turning extrinsic motivation intrinsic has allowed countless players to go beyond their limits and dominate their opponents. Steve Smith might have had the largest chip ever. Standing at just 5’9” and weighing under 200 pounds, Smith was overlooked by major college programs. He started his collegiate career at Santa Monica College before transferring to Utah for his junior campaign. Smith immediately made an impact, especially on special teams, scoring 11 total touchdowns including an NCAA high three punt return touchdowns. His senior season in 2000 was not as spectacular, but he still averaged over 20 yards per reception.

The lack of definitive improvement from his junior season to his senior year led to him dropping down draft boards, which turned out to be incredibly lucky for the Carolina Panthers. In the 2001 NFL Draft, the Panthers took Dan Morgan in the first round, Kris Jenkins in the second, and finally took Smith in the third round. Despite major pundits like The Sporting News declaring that the team wasted a third round pick on a guy who would just be a punt returner, Smith became a dominant force on the offense just as the other two became dominant pieces for Carolina’s defense. The pundits weren’t wrong about Smith’s impact on special teams, either. On his first career touch, Smith took the opening kickoff of the 2001 season against the Minnesota Vikings 93 yards for a touchdown, one of three return touchdowns his rookie year (two kickoff returns, one punt return). Smith ended up being one of the few bright spots in that doomed 2001 season, earning Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro honors as a returner.

The 2002 season showed flashes of what would come from the wide receiver Steve Smith. Paired up with Muhsin Muhammad, the duo put up some decent stats despite less than stellar quarterback play. As was the case for most Panthers, it was 2003 that really shone a spotlight on Smith’s talent. He exploded onto the scene with 88 catches for 1,110 yards and seven touchdowns, adding another punt return touchdown for good measure. His impact went beyond the box score, however, as he became new quarterback Jake Delhomme’s favorite target. The unforgettable Super Bowl run was largely driven by a dominant defense, but Smith provided the offensive fireworks necessary for the team to advance. His 32 yard touchdown catch in the third quarter of the Wild Card game against the Dallas Cowboys all but sealed the win for the Panthers, his now infamous 69 yard “X-Clown” touchdown reception in double overtime against the Rams pushed the team into the NFC Championship Game, and he added a game-tying 39 yard touchdown in the second quarter of the Super Bowl.

While the Panthers would not see team success of that nature for another dozen years, Smith blossomed into one of the best wide receivers in the NFL. Despite breaking his leg in the first game of the 2004 season, he returned at full strength in 2005, winning the receiving triple crown (though only tied for first in receiving touchdowns). His line of 103 catches for 1.563 yards and 12 touchdowns were video game numbers. Those 103 catches would be Panthers single season records until some guy named Christian McCaffrey came along seven years later, and the 1,563 receiving yards is still a Panthers record. For the second time in his five year career, Smith was named to the Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro roster while also taking home the Comeback Player of the Year Award. He would go on to make three more Pro Bowls (2006, 2008, and 2011) and a Second Team All Pro nod in 2008. With the arrival of new Face of the Franchise Cam Newton, Smith struggled to take on more of a secondary role. While his production was still bordering on elite until 2013, there was always an undercurrent of strife between him and Cam. That sense of locker room distraction combined with the Panthers wanting to get younger and cheaper at the position led to the team releasing Smith in March of 2014. Two days later, he signed with the Baltimore Ravens. He would end up playing three years with the Ravens, even eclipsing the thousand yard mark in 2014. Smith’s contract with the Ravens expired in 2017, and a lack of interest from other teams led to his retirement.

Steve Smith’s legacy in Carolina goes well beyond stats, though he holds some incredible receiving marks in Panthers history: he’s the all-time Panthers leader in targets (1,438), catches (836), yards (12,197), touchdowns (67), and yards per game (67). He also leads the team in punt returns (178), punt return yards (1,652), punt return touchdowns (4), and longest punt return (87 yards), while finishing second only to Michael Bates in kickoff returns (98), kickoff return yards (2,371), and kickoff return touchdowns (2). Smith finished his career in the top ten in NFL history in all-purpose yards and should be a Hall of Famer at some point. But it’s not the numbers that matter to Panthers fans, it’s the moments: X-Clown, the 2006 playoff game against the Bears, the sideline quotes, the touchdown celebrations, breaking his arm and still scoring a touchdown against the Giants in 2009, grabbing Malcom Jenkins and dragging him by the facemask after scoring a touchdown against the Saints in 2011, and even (unfortunately) the “blood and guts” game against the Panthers in 2014. Despite all the numbers he racked up on the field, the only number that matters at the end of the day to Panthers fans? 89. Bottom line.

item.title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: It begins with Pirates
item.description: So it begins.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL season is here. The wait is over.

The Cincinnati Bengals will take the field Sunday at Paycor Stadium against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a game that actually matters.

And it does matter.

Unlike the MLB or the NBA, which both have absurdly long regular seasons, the NFL (for now) plays only 17 games. That means every game—from the first to the last—is important. The Bengals are contenders, and if they want the road to the AFC Championship to go through Cincinnati, they can’t afford to take games off.

Cincy has an easy schedule this year. While I don’t think the Bucs are one of the best teams in the league, I do think they’re a top-five team the Bengals will face. I also think the Bengals are better than the Buccaneers, especially on offense.

There aren’t many defenses in the league that can consistently keep up with Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and the ridiculous number of weapons at Burrow’s disposal.

And I think the Bengals’ much-improved defense will make at least a stop or two.

Having said all that, I don’t expect the Bengals’ offense to be in midseason form right out of the gate. Any supercar needs a couple of laps to warm up.

I was also wrong about Baker Mayfield.

When he was drafted, I thought he was a clown. And, from the outside looking in, pretty much anything happening in Cleveland resembles a burning dumpster. But once Mayfield got out of there, my opinion started to change. He’s since revitalized his career, and he’s become a pretty hard guy not to root for.

Except for this week.

He’ll be able to move the ball against the Bengals, and Tampa Bay has enough offensive firepower to make Cincinnati pay for mistakes.

The unsung hero for the Bengals could be Chase Brown.

If I’m a defensive coordinator facing the Burrow-Chase-Higgins trifecta, I’m focusing the vast majority of my attention on them. Chase has to be doubled almost all the time, and Higgins can’t consistently be left one-on-one either. Then there’s a third receiver, Mike Gesicki, Erick All Jr., or somebody else waiting to take advantage.

The fact is, if the offensive line gives Burrow time to throw, someone is going to get open.

That leaves Tampa Bay with two basic options: put as many defensive backs on the field as possible, or pin their ears back and try to get to Burrow before one of his weapons gets open.

That’s where Brown could come in.

If the Buccaneers load up on defensive backs, Brown could take advantage of a lighter box. And one of the best ways to slow down an aggressive pass rush is to make it pay with an effective running game.

I don’t think the Bengals need to “establish the run” to set up the pass, but it’d certainly be nice to see them punish defenses for selling out to stop Burrow. They’ve spent a lot of time working with Burrow under center and adding more play action into the offense. If they can pull that off effectively, it could buy Burrow the extra second he needs to find one of his many weapons downfield.

The guy the Bengals’ offense needs to keep an eye on is Rueben Bain Jr.

Had the Bengals not traded the No. 10 overall pick to the Giants for Dexter Lawrence II, Bain is the guy I would have wanted Cincinnati to select.

As it turns out, they’ll face him in Week 1.

There hasn’t been a Buccaneers defender with double-digit sacks since the 2021 season, and they’re hoping Bain can help snap that streak. The Bengals would probably prefer he starts his push in Week 2.

For Cincinnati’s defense, all eyes are on the defensive line.

Last year, the starters were B.J. Hill and T.J. Slaton. Now, Hill and Slaton are the backups, while Lawrence and Jonathan Allen are starting. Throw in Kris Jenkins and rookie Landon Robinson, and suddenly the Bengals have a deep and talented defensive interior—something they’ve desperately lacked over the last few seasons.

That group could make all the difference Sunday.

If the Bengals can get consistent pressure from Boye Mafe and Myles Murphy while Lawrence, Allen and company collapse the pocket from the interior, Mayfield could be forced to get rid of the ball early or throw off-platform. That creates opportunities for Cincinnati’s linebackers and defensive backs to make plays.

So, whose defense steps up the most?

Vegas lists the Bengals as 3.5-point favorites, which is basically home-field advantage plus another half-point.

I’ll take those odds.

I see a close game that is somewhat frustrating at times. It’s Week 1. There will probably be some rust, some missed opportunities, and at least one moment that makes Bengals fans collectively wonder why they allow this team to do this to them every year.

But I think Cincinnati wins.

Bengals 27, Buccaneers 20.

It might not be pretty, but being 1-0 is all that matters.

Who do you think wins? Sound off!

Who Dey, and welcome to what we will hopefully look back on as the first game of the greatest season in Bengals franchise history!

item.title: Dark horse Jovaughn Gwyn wins Ravens’ Week 1 starting center job
item.description: The Ravens have named Jovaughn Gwyn as their starting center for Week 1 vs. the Colts.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter announced that Jovaughn Gwyn would start at center for the 2026 regular-season opener against the Indianapolis Colts.

“ I would say that’s a Week 1 decision — not necessarily a permanent decision,” Minter added, noting that former Browns starter Ethan Pocic was “still coming back” from a torn Achilles suffered last December.

Gwyn, 27, will now make his first career start against the Colts’ ferocious defensive tackle duo of DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart. This will be an early test for offensive coordinator Declan Doyle’s new scheme and quarterback Lamar Jackson’s command of it at the line of scrimmage.

The Ravens’ starting center competition was one of the team’s biggest offseason storylines following Tyler Linderbaum’s departure in free agency. Gwyn was seen as a dark horse after spending three years in Atlanta with offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who had a loud voice in The Castle this offseason. Former Colts backup Danny Pinter seemed to take an early lead in spring practices, and Pocic’s arrival in July threatened to push Gwyn to the third string once he was healthy.

But Gwyn’s standout performance in the Ravens’ first preseason game against the Eagles and Pinter’s season-ending knee injury during joint practices in Minnesota propelled him into the first team. Pocic still got plenty of playing time across the last two preseason games, but he never did enough to displace Gwyn. Minter’s comments also indicate that Pocic is not back at 100% and could factor into the picture later in the season.

Gwyn could preempt that with a strong start to the year, especially against such stiff competition. Beyond blocking Buckner and Stewart, he will have to cover all of the mental aspects of the center position. His ability to read the defense and communicate the calls in partnership with Jackson at the line of scrimmage will be crucial.

The Ravens’ decision is another sign of Ledford’s influence within the organization. The team declined to trade up for a center on Day 2 or select one of the several Power Four starters who were available on Day 3, instead trusting their new offensive line coach to coach up one of their other options. Among them was Gwyn, a 2023 seventh-round pick out of South Carolina who Ledford developed in Atlanta and brought with him to Baltimore this offseason. Gwyn stayed on the Falcons’ practice squad for two years before earning the backup center job in 2025.

Early struggles from Gwyn would be a significant problem for the Ravens offense. They would also offer a glimpse at Minter’s in-season management style. Would he be quick to replace Gwyn with Pocic, or would he fall into the past regime’s frustrating pattern of leaving subpar blockers on the field for far too long? The new head coach has preached standards and accountability since he arrived in Baltimore; that would be a chance to practice them. The Ravens, of course, will be hoping that situation never comes up.

It is worth noting that Gwyn is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent this offseason – as is Pocic – so Minter’s mention of a non-permanent decision also (perhaps inadvertently) references the team’s lack of a long-term at the center position.

But for at least one week, it will be Gwyn snapping the ball to Jackson when the Ravens offense takes the field.

item.title: Rams vs. 49ers will be a mini Super Bowl for Melbourne's iconic cricket ground
item.description: The Rams and 49ers kick off the NFL season 8,000 miles from home, turning the Melbourne Cricket Ground into the stage for Australia's first regular-season NFL game.
item.content:encoded:
The Melbourne Cricket Ground has played host to soccer friendlies for decades, exhibition matches with nothing on the line. No stakes, no standings.

What happens this week is the opposite, an NFL opener between the Rams and San Francisco 49ers. The bad blood is real. It’s an undeniable unfriendly.

No better place to stage a NFC West showdown 8,000 miles from home than a venue that’s a cricket cathedral, a centerpiece of the 1956 Olympic Games, and the site of three sold-out Eras Tour concerts that drew 96,000 Swifties per night.

Read more:Rams revel in Aaron Donald’s comeback, but he might not suit up for opener

Now, for the first time, the NFL is preparing to unveil a regular-season game Down Under.

“It’s an ambitious, bold plan,” said Stuart Fox, chief executive of the Melbourne Cricket Club.

“We weren’t sure the NFL would fly this far given their international schedule. It’s a huge thrill. The excitement shows in ticket demand; it was pretty much sold out straight away. As we get closer to the date, the excitement keeps building.”

The timing is a challenge, and not just for the Rams and 49ers. The date falls in the middle of the Australian rules football finals, and it’s likely the MCG — affectionately nicknamed “The G” — will host a match in the twilight slot on Saturday evening, roughly 24 hours after the NFL rivals play. (49ers-Rams will take place on Thursday night in the U.S.)

That means replacing turf, putting down new field markings, taking down the goal posts, cleaning the entire place and the like. In cricket terms, it’s a sticky wicket.

“Thousands of staff will work through the night,” Fox said. “It’s the tightest turnaround in MCG history. Getting it right matters, because the AFL finals are one of the most important times of the year for us.”

Fox said the plan is to do a considerable amount of turf replacement, but not because he expects the pristine grass to take a beating from the cleats of massive humans.

“It’s because of the NFL’s extensive line markings,” he said. “The NFL loves its paint, especially in the end zones. Those sections get pulled up, new turf goes down, and we’re playing on it again within 24 hours.”

Unlike a football stadium, the MCG has a huge, oval-shaped field, which means there will be more perimeter space around the playing surface. Surely, that will be consumed by production equipment as the NFL is treating this game like a mini-Super Bowl, complete with the Jonas Brothers performing at halftime.

“We’re building an unforgettable experience for fans, and having an internationally renowned act like the Jonas Brothers perform at halftime reinforces the scale and significance of this historic event,” Charlotte Offord, the NFL’s general manager of Australia and New Zealand said in a news release. “We can’t wait to welcome our fans from across Australia and beyond for a truly world-class celebration of sport and entertainment.”

Naturally, the game will have an Australian flair, with concession stands selling meat pies with tomato sauce (essentially ketchup), sausage rolls, hot chips, along with hot dogs. High-end coffee options, too, as that’s a point of pride for Melbourne.

Not bad for a venue that has occupied its current site since 1853, land that was once used for police-force horse paddocks and is a short, happy walk from downtown Melbourne.

Come to think of it, not unfriendly at all.

item.title: Cowboys news: All eyes on T.J. Bass stepping in for Tyler Smith at LG
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys are going to be without all-world left guard Tyler Smith for at least the first four weeks of the season, something head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced on Monday. Coach Schotty also confirmed it will be T.J. Bass starting in Smith’s spot.

The biggest phase of the game the Cowboys will miss Smith in is his run blocking, with the Cowboys also counting on a repeat performance by Javonte Williams at running back, and sorting out the pecking order behind with Malik Davis and Emari Demercado.

Cowboys LG Tyler Smith to undergo thumb surgery, miss 4-6 weeks – Nick Shook, NFL.com

A huge blow to the Cowboys offensive line just ahead of two divisional games to start the season.

The three-time Pro Bowl guard and cornerstone of Dallas’ interior offensive line was not seen at Monday’s practice, leading to questions regarding his status. With the entire regular season ahead and the thumb injury limiting Smith, the guard felt now was the best time to have the issue fixed, per Schottenheimer.

“Just at the end of the day, he felt like he couldn’t do the things he had to do at a high level,” the coach said Monday. “We know this is a long season. It’s unfortunate but that’s why we coveted T.J. Bass and having T.J. Bass back. I think he’s played a lot of really good football for us, and we expect that he’ll continue to do so.”

Cowboys have a ‘ton of confidence’ in T.J. Bass filling in for Tyler Smith – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

T.J. Bass has been called on and played well before, and the Cowboys will need more of it as he starts the season at left guard.

During training camp, Bass would often times get work with the first-team offensive line in team drills when Schottenheimer and the Cowboys staff would give Smith less snaps in order to manage his workload as a veteran. Schottenheimer hopes those reps will pay off in a game setting.

“Offensive line play is tied together,” Schottenheimer said. “We’ve gone into games with four new starters on the offensive line. I’m very, very confident that this group will play well against a really good front. I have great confidence in T.J. Bass. He’s extremely bright, very physical, great athlete. He’ll do a marvelous job for us, I’m sure, stepping in.”

What T.J. Bass’ stats tell us about replacing Tyler Smith – Brandon Loree, Blogging The Boys

Bass is a player the team can trust to not allow quarterback Dak Prescott to take unnecessary hits.

Despite average overall stats for his position, the Cowboys could hang their hat on how efficient Bass was in limited reps. He started in games against the Green Bay Packers, New York Jets, Carolina Panthers, Los Angeles Chargers, and Washington Commanders.

He allowed zero sacks last year (T-1st among all 82 guards), had four pressures allowed (second best), and a 99.0 pass-blocking efficiency grade (first). A small sample size to be sure, but he acquitted himself very well.

Brian Schottenheimer raises important question about Cowboys offense by answering another – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports

Not having Tyler Smith at left guard will put a bigger magnifying glass on Tyler Guyton at left tackle, who the Cowboys will need to stay healthy to avoid going into the further depths of their OL backups.

This is a big mystery for a Cowboys offense preparing to start a left tackle who has dealt with injuries in his first couple of NFL seasons. It’s a significant question, and Dallas does not have a firm answer right now.

When push comes to shove, I think the Cowboys would end up giving Jones a shot at left tackle. But right now it doesn’t sound like they’re giving him swing tackle treatment. 

Emari Demercado may be more than just the Cowboys’ third RB – Jess Haynie, The Landry Hat

It will be fun to see how RB Emari Demercado’s role develops as the season goes on.

When Dallas added Demercado, his profile immediately sounds like a prototypical backup for Javonte Williams. He’s a patient runner with good vision, not adverse to contact while also having breakaway speed. He’s also a proficient receiver and pass blocker, both especially valuable for whoever spells Williams on third-down plays.

Demercado is also noted as a “four-core” special teams player, meaning he can play on every unit. This is also a positive point on Davis’ resume, further showing their similarity.

Giants cut Darius Slayton – Michael David Smith, Pro Football Talk

A roster move for Dallas’ week one opponent ahead of Sunday night.

The move comes as a surprise if only because of Slayton’s contract: Just last year, he signed a three-year, $36 million contract, and he is guaranteed $9.75 million this year. Cutting him only saves the Giants $2.5 million, but apparently they’re down enough on him that they thought that savings was worth sending him packing.

The Giants presumably tried to trade Slayton before cutting him and found that no one wanted to trade for that contract.

item.title: How the Rams turned their weakest link into a strength with secondary makeover
item.description: After the Seattle Seahawks shredded them, the Rams responded by overhauling the secondary, trading for All-Pro Trent McDuffie and signing Jaylen Watson.
item.content:encoded:
Blockbuster trades and high-profile free-agent signings have been Rams trademarks during the Sean McVay era, but success also has been built on more subtle transactions.

After the Seattle Seahawks exposed the secondary — and especially cornerbacks — in the Rams’ NFC championship game defeat last season, McVay and Rams general manager Les Snead took steps to upgrade a unit they left unchanged from 2024.

Last March, a few days after trading for All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie, they signed McDuffie’s former Kansas City Chiefs teammate, cornerback Jaylen Watson.

The moves turned the Rams’ weakest link into one of their strongest.

“Rare opportunities presented themselves to be able to get both Trent and Jaylen,” McVay said Sunday. “I didn’t think that would be a situation that we would be able to pull off, just based on kind of how we had that spot slotted.”

The acquisitions of McDuffie and Watson completed an overhaul of the secondary that began by keeping an important piece in place: safety Quentin Lake received an extension in January that included $25 million in guarantees. In March, the team agreed to terms with safety Kam Curl on an extension that includes $24 million in guarantees.

Then came the major move: The Rams traded the 29th pick in the draft and three future draft picks for McDuffie, and then signed him to a then-record contract that includes $100 million in guarantees.

Jimmy Lake, who replaced Aubrey Pleasant as the Rams’ defensive backs coach, recruited McDuffie when he played at St. John Bosco High. Lake coached McDuffie at the University of Washington.

And he watched McDuffie become an All-Pro and two-time Super Bowl champion with the Chiefs.

So when McVay pulled Jimmy Lake aside and told him that the Rams were trading for McDuffie, Lake said he was nearly stunned.

And thrilled.

“I was like, ‘Wow,’” Lake said. “We just got a dawg.”

A few days later they signed Watson to a deal that includes $34 million in guarantees.

“Once they got Trent, I was like, ‘He got two cornerbacks money, so they’re probably not going to get another one,’” Watson said. “So I thought I was going to go back to the Chiefs. But it ended up working out. When they called I was excited.”

So was Curl.

“It was like rumors of it being an emphasis,” Curl said of the Rams remaking the secondary. “But then they showed it was true.”

Now, as the Rams prepare for their season opener against the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, the secondary is regarded as a pillar for a team that also traded for defensive end Myles Garrett and welcomed back legendary lineman Aaron Donald from a two-year retirement.

“Just so many different looks we can give teams,” Watson said of a secondary that also includes cornerbacks Emmanuel Forbes Jr. and Josh Wallace and safeties Kam Kinchens and Jaylen McCollough. “You’re not going to know who’s where because we can move so many different people around.

Read more:Plaschke: Rams will go undefeated on their way to winning another home Super Bowl title

“It’s a fun defense to watch. I enjoy watching it as much as I enjoy playing in it.”

Quentin Lake said he anticipated changes after the Rams lost to the Seahawks, who won the Super Bowl with a talented secondary led by All-Pro cornerback Devon Witherspoon.

Lake pointed to the Rams’ 2021 team that won Super Bowl LVI with lockdown defensive back Jalen Ramsey paired with a dominating Donald.

“You’re able to dictate the terms up front and also shut one side down on the field,” Lake said.

The Rams now deploy McDuffie with Garrett and Donald.

McDuffie is happy to be back in Southern California and has easily melded into the Rams’ culture.

Read more:'We’re like the new Dodgers.' Rams know it's another Super Bowl-or-bust season

“I wasn’t trying to come in here and say, ‘We need to go this way or that way,’ or things I try to say over in Kansas City,’” he said during training camp. “Nah, it’s a clean slate. Let’s come in, let’s build with each other.”

The defensive backs bonded on the field before and during practices and while playing card games in their dorm rooms during camp.

McDuffie’s attitude and skill set, and the toughness and “swag” that Watson plays with are palpable, Jimmy Lake said.

“We definitely feel the extra surge of attitude and awareness,” he said. “That’s infectious throughout the whole secondary, and the whole defense.”

item.title: Who will be the first Detroit Lion to record a sack in 2026?
item.description: Which player on the Detroit Lions defense will record the first sack of the 2026 season?
item.content:encoded:
Nothing gets the home crowd hyped up quite like a quarterback sack. With the Detroit Lions hosting the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 of the 2026 season, Ford Field will be eager to see Tyler Shough hit the turf—preferably multiple times.

Despite the Lions lacking pass rush last season, they still finished tied for fourth in the league with 49 sacks. Part of this came from consistency. The Lions had five games with four or more sacks, yet they also recorded seven games with one or fewer sacks. Too often it was feast or famine for Detroit.

Aidan Hutchinson led the way for the team, recording 14.5 sacks on the season. Perhaps surprisingly, it was Al-Quadin Muhammad coming in second with 11.0 sacks. However, his season was another example of that inconsistent pass rush. Despite playing in all 17 games, 7.5 of his sacks came in just three games—across the remaining 14 games, he had just 3.5 sacks.

With Muhammad departing for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in free agency, the Lions were looking for running mates for Hutchinson. They signed DJ Wonnum and added Derrick Moore and Skyler Gill-Howard via the draft. Coupled with Alim McNeill, Levi Onwuzurike, and Ahmed Hassanein returning from injury, the Lions are hoping their front seven can provide a much-needed upgrade in the pass rush department.

Which member of the Lions defense will be the first one to bring down an opposing quarterback?

Who will be the first Detroit Lion to record a sack in 2026?

Today’s Question of the Day is:

My answer: Jack Campbell.

There is no question that Hutchinson should lead the team in sacks by the end of the season, but early on, I expect opponents to focus on stopping him. I am optimistic about how McNeill, Wonnum, Moore, and Tyleik Williams can perform in this defense, but none of them command the attention that Hutchinson does. I am expecting double teams and chip blocks early and often for Hutchinson.

Of the linemen expected to play a majority of snaps, the two names that stand out the most are McNeill and Wonnum. McNeill has looked like his old self in training camp, while Wonnum should be a reliable contributor on early downs. However, given that this could be a run-happy Saints offense, pass rush opportunities could be somewhat limited—I would not be surprised if the Saints drop back fewer than 20 times in Week 1. If the Lions are focused on stopping the run, the primary role of McNeill and Wonnum could be to plug gaps and hold contain, not rush the passer. I also want to tip my hat to the Saints offensive line, a unit that I think is better than advertised—I really liked their signing of David Edwards to shore up their weakest position, left guard.

That is why I think Campbell could record the first Lions sack of the season. We know how potent he can be as a blitzer, and I expect Kelvin Sheppard’s defense to get creative with timely blitzes. Because of how versatile Campbell is as a linebacker, predicting where he will be on each snap is a nightmare for offensive coordinators. Whether he is stopping the run, dropping into coverage, rushing up the middle, or spying the quarterback, he demonstrated in 2025 that he can do it all. I think there is a good chance that a Campbell blitz could go unnoticed and result in a big-time play.

Sure, we could talk about which team is going to win the Super Bowl in February. But we know what you'll really be talking about at halftime this Sunday afternoon.

Don't worry, we have you covered.

Covers surveyed over 5,000 NFL fans to find out who they thought is the most attractive team leader ahead of the new season, and while the top pick may not surprise anyone… there’s some shocks ahead in the top 5 and bottom 5…

Key Takeaways

  • The Runaway Winner: Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams absolutely dominated the survey, receiving nearly 16% of the votes. The Rams' coach scored nearly double the amount of votes gained by the runner-up, Green Bay’s Matt LaFleur.
  • Crossing Rival Lines: When breaking down the top attractive pick by each fan base, Sean McVay was the number one choice for fans of 12 different teams.
  • The Bottom of the Pack: New York Jets head coach, Aaron Glenn received the fewest votes across the entire league, coming in last with just 0.60% of the vote. They were closely followed by Tampa Bay, Las Vegas, and Cleveland.
  • Supported vs. Attractive Discrepancy: Despite the Dallas Cowboys being the most heavily supported team in this survey, their head coach garnered comparatively little attention in the attractiveness poll, receiving the 16th most votes.

The Hot Parade: The NFL’s Top 5 Most Attractive Head Coaches According to Fans

1. Sean McVay | Los Angeles Rams

  • Universal Appeal Over Homerism: An incredible95% of the near-800 votes for the Rams' head coach came from outside fanbases. Only 40 of his votes were actually from Rams fans.
  • The Cowboys and Steelers Swoon: Fans of the Dallas Cowboys and Pittsburgh Steelers actually found the Rams' coach more attractive than his own fanbase did.
  • NFC West Betrayals: He pulled heavily from massive divisional rivals, securing 28 votes from Seattle Seahawks fans and 21 from San Francisco 49ers fans, who were perfectly happy to cross enemy lines.

Why you might find Sean McVay attractive: His flawless hair gel consistency is perfectly matched by a photographic, savant-level memory capable of recalling every intermediate crossing route designed since 2017.

2. Matt LaFleur | Green Bay Packers

  • The NFC North’s Guilty Pleasure: Despite the famously bitter "Black and Blue" division rivalries, 24 fans from the rest of the NFC North cast their ballot for Green Bay. This included 10 votes from Detroit Lions fans and 9 votes from Chicago Bears fans.
  • Fierce Hometown Loyalty:Packers fans are highly protective of their coach's looks. Over 54% of all Packers fans surveyed voted for their own guy, generating 68 of his 208 total votes.

Why you might find Matt LaFleur attractive: He possesses the pristine, catalog-ready jawline of a movie star seamlessly paired with the hyper-analytical brain of an offensive mastermind.

3. Mike Macdonald | Seattle Seahawks

  • The Baltimore Reunion: The Seahawks' coach received a very specific bump from Baltimore Ravens fans (9 votes). This is a great statistical quirk, considering he just left his role as the Ravens' defensive coordinator to take the top job in Seattle.
  • Strong Local Foundation: Coming in as the 3rd most attractive coach in the league overall (163 votes), he enjoyed strong support at home. Over 53% of surveyed Seahawks fans selected him as their number one choice.

Why you might find Mike Macdonald attractive: His boy-genius charm lies entirely in his ability to completely disguise his true intentions until your relationship hits a third-and-long situation.

4. Nick Sirianni | Philadelphia Eagles

  • NFC East Enemies Agree: Even amidst arguably the most toxic division rivalry in sports, 11 Dallas Cowboys fans and 6 New York Giants fans swallowed their pride and admitted the Eagles' coach is the most attractive in the league.
  • Heavy Philadelphia Bias: The Philadelphia Eagles' coach relied heavily on hometown backing. Nearly half of his total votes (46.9%) came purely from Philadelphia fans, who showed up in numbers to support their guy.

Why you might find Nick Sirianni attractive: You love a chaotic bad boy who will passionately defend your honor, scream at opposing fans, and treat a casual date night like the fourth quarter of the NFC Championship.

5. Andy Reid | Kansas City Chiefs

  • Super Bowl Rematch Romance: The Kansas City Chiefs' coach pulled in 19 votes from Philadelphia Eagles fans (the team he famously beat in Super Bowl LVII, and previously coached) and 18 votes from San Francisco 49ers fans (who he defeated in Super Bowls LIV and LVIII).
  • Carried by the League, Not Locals: Despite securing 292 votes overall (placing him 5th in the entire NFL), only 28% of Chiefs fans actually voted for him. He was carried into the top 5 by widespread, quiet admiration from 27 other fanbases.

Why you might find Andy Reid attractive: He is the ultimate Hawaiian-shirt-wearing comfort choice, offering unmatched long term relationship stability and the soothing guarantee that he will always let you order the extra appetizers.

A Bunch Of Guys With Great Personalities: The 5 Least Attractive NFL Head Coaches According to Fans

28. Shane Steichen | Indianapolis Colts

  • Low Hometown Confidence: Only 10% of the surveyed Indianapolis Colts fans selected their own coach as the most attractive.
  • The Philly Connection: Steichen managed to pull in votes from Philadelphia Eagles fans, which could be lingering affection from his highly successful stint as their offensive coordinator.
  • Minimal Rivalry Respect: He only pulled a single vote from the rest of the AFC South, thanks to one lone Tennessee Titans fan.

Why you might find Shane Steichen attractive: You are captivated by the rugged, sleepless efficiency of a man who skips the flashy media campaigns to focus entirely on designing the perfect playbook for your heart.

29. Todd Monken | Cleveland Browns

  • Lack of Local Love: Monken struggled with his new fanbase in this survey; only9.1% of surveyed Cleveland Browns fans cast a vote for him.
  • A Ravens Reunion: Among his 21 total votes, he managed to pull exactly 1 vote from a Baltimore Ravens fan: a fun nod to his recent time serving as the Ravens' offensive coordinator before taking the top job in Cleveland.

Why you might find Todd Monken attractive: He has the blunt, seasoned charm of a football pirate who won't hesitate to give you the unvarnished truth before drawing up a gorgeous vertical passing concept to make up for it.

30. Klint Kubiak | Las Vegas Raiders

  • The AFC West Sweep: Despite his very low overall total of 40 votes, he accomplished a rare and amusing feat: he received exactly one vote from each of his AFC West division rivals: one from a Chiefs fan, one from a Broncos fan, and one from a Chargers fan.
  • Heavy Reliance on the Black Hole: Unlike the top-tier coaches who were carried by widespread league appeal, nearly half of Kubiak's votes (45%) came purely from Las Vegas Raiders loyalists.

Why you might find Klint Kubiak attractive: He exudes the quiet, disciplined confidence of a man carrying elite wide-zone blocking DNA who values flawless execution over flash.

31. Todd Bowles | Tampa Bay Buccaneers

  • NFC South Shutout: The Buccaneers' head coach received exactly zero votes from any of his bitter NFC South division rivals (the Falcons, Panthers, and Saints shut him out entirely).
  • A Random Assortment: His 35 total votes were scattered very thinly across the league, with his highest outside support coming from just 2 votes each from Pittsburgh Steelers and New York Giants fans.

Why you might find Todd Bowles attractive: You want a partner with a legendary poker face who remains calm and completely unbothered even if the world is burning down around him.

32. Aaron Glenn | New York Jets

  • Dead Last: Sitting at the very bottom of the entire survey with just 29 votes, Glenn captured the attention of only 11.6% of surveyed NY Jets fans.
  • The Lone Patriot: In the notoriously vicious AFC East, he did manage to wring out exactly 1 vote from a New England Patriots fan.
  • Saints Supporter: He pulled in 2 votes from New Orleans Saints fans, potentially a holdover from his years serving as the Saints' defensive backs coach.

Why you might find Aaron Glenn attractive: His relentless optimism and gritty, leader-of-men energy make you want to run through a literal brick wall for him despite the chaos surrounding your relationship.

Out of the 5,022 fans surveyed, roughly29.3% of respondents selected the head coach of their own supported team as the most attractive. Maybe they’re a big fan of anyone wearing their team colours?

Why are some coaches considered more attractive than others?

While it’s undeniable that Sean McVay is an All-American hotty: some of the more surprising entries in the top ten tell us there may be more to ‘attractiveness’ than just good looks.

Unless, you know, we as a people are actually really into the smell of barbecue sauce and ‘Big Santa Energy’.

The Halo Effect of Championship Success

Success is inherently attractive. When a coach wins, they exude confidence, command respect, and are constantly filmed smiling in celebratory moments.

  • 💍 Recent Super Bowl Exposure: The Kansas City Chiefs, Philadelphia Eagles and Los Angeles Rams have dominated recent Super Bowl broadcasts. Head coaches who are constantly associated with triumph, confetti, and the pinnacle of the sport naturally benefit from a massive, positive psychological bias.
  • 🏈 The Quarterback Proximity: Coaches attached to elite, face-of-the-franchise quarterbacks (like Patrick Mahomes or Matthew Stafford) get to ride the coattails of their team's massive offensive success, making the head coach appear more in control and appealing on the sidelines.

The "Offensive Genius" Aura & Advanced Analytics

The modern NFL fetishizes the "offensive guru." Coaches who are perceived as intellectually superior or who heavily utilize advanced sports analytics and quantitative metrics carry a distinct swagger.

  • 🧠 Play-Calling Prestige: Coaches who are highly rated in this survey (like Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan) are consistently celebrated by the media for their complex, data-driven play designs.
  • 💡 The Intelligence Premium: Fans often conflate high-level strategic intelligence with attractiveness. A coach who is consistently praised on broadcasts for outsmarting the defense gains an "aura" that transcends physical looks.

Front-Office Competence & Organizational Stability

A head coach never operates in a vacuum. The infrastructure around them drastically alters how they are perceived by the public.

  • 🎯 Drafting Success Rates: A coach whose general manager consistently hits on high draft picks will always look better on the podium. They inherit talented rosters that make their jobs easier, greatly reducing visible stress.
  • 💰 Financial Cost-Per-Win: When a front office is highly efficient and normalizes cost-per-win metrics effectively, the team operates like a well-oiled machine. Coaches in stable, well-managed organizations look composed and relaxed, whereas coaches in dysfunctional organizations often look visibly aged, tense, and exhausted.

Media Footprint and Prime-Time Saturation

The volume of a coach's exposure dictates their familiarity, and the psychological "mere-exposure effect" dictates that people tend to develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them.

  • 📺 National TV Placements: Teams like the Cowboys, Packers, and Chiefs are consistently scheduled for Sunday Night, Monday Night, and late-afternoon marquee slots. Their coaches get significantly more high-definition, prime-time camera time than a coach buried in regional 1:00 PM broadcasts.
  • 📈 Market-Implied Probabilities: As teams become favorites in prediction markets to win their division or the Super Bowl, the media narrative shifts to hyper-focus on their leadership. This constant, positive media profiling acts as free PR for the coach's public image.

The "Hot Seat" Stress Toll

Conversely, losing actively detracts from a coach's physical appeal.

  • 😰 The Visible Stress: Coaches at the very bottom of the attractiveness poll (like Aaron Glenn) are often battling through difficult rebuilding phases, intense media scrutiny, and job insecurity. The visible toll of 80-hour work weeks combined with a losing record manifests in poor posture, unkempt appearances, and defensive press conferences.
